modules.name: Digital Finance Regulatory Perimeter
modules.novelty_rationale: Prudential oversight is extending beyond regulated financial entities to concentrated technology providers and crypto firms, and allowing banks to custody digital assets, shifting the perimeter from traditional intermediaries to digital infrastructure and assets.
modules.reasoning: Implications 2, 3, 5, and 6 form a coherent subsystem of regulatory perimeter expansion into digital infrastructure and digital-asset activities. They share a transmission path in which operational failures, concentration in critical ICT providers, and digital-asset volatility are brought under supervisory scrutiny to prevent spillovers into banks and the wider financial system through common infrastructure, counterparty linkages, and bank balance sheets.

evidence_signals.title: EU Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) applies from 17 January 2025
evidence_signals.content: From 17 January 2025, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 on digital operational resilience for the financial sector (DORA) and its technical standards apply across the EU, without a transitional period. DORA covers a wide range of financial entities, from credit and payment institutions to insurers, fund managers and crypto-asset service providers, and rests on five pillars: ICT risk management, classification and reporting of major ICT-related incidents, digital operational resilience testing including threat-led penetration testing, management of ICT third-party risk, and information sharing. Financial entities must be able to report major ICT incidents from day one and must submit registers of information on their contractual arrangements with ICT third-party providers, which competent authorities forward to the European Supervisory Authorities by 30 April 2025. On this basis the ESAs will designate critical ICT third-party providers, such as large cloud service providers, for direct EU oversight; the first designations are expected in the second half of 2025. In December 2024 the ESAs had urged entities to close remaining gaps, as several standards were finalised only late.

evidence_signals.title: FSB Work Programme for 2025
evidence_signals.content: The FSB published its Work Programme for 2025 on 23 January 2025, outlining key regulatory and financial stability priorities for the year. Priority areas: (1) Supporting global cooperation on financial stability; (2) Enhancing resilience of non-bank financial intermediation (NBFI) while preserving its benefits – major G20 deliverable; (3) Harnessing benefits of digital innovation (crypto-assets, AI in finance, cross-border payments) while containing risks – major G20 deliverable; (4) Implementing the systemically important financial institution (SIFI) framework; (5) Addressing financial risks from climate change – climate roadmap progress; (6) Enhancing cross-border payments; (7) Completing resolution reforms. Key G20 deliverables planned: NBFI leverage policy recommendations (Jul 2025); Vulnerabilities from AI in finance (Oct 2025); Thematic peer review on crypto-assets (Oct 2025); FSB Annual Report (Dec 2025). Context: FSB is chaired by Klaas Knot (DNB). Secretariat in Basel, hosted by BIS.

evidence_signals.title: US Executive Order 14178 'Strengthening American Leadership in Digital Financial Technology' prohibits a US CBDC
evidence_signals.content: On 23 January 2025 the US President signed Executive Order 14178, setting the policy of the new administration to 'support the responsible growth and use of digital assets, blockchain technology, and related technologies across all sectors of the economy'. The order prohibits agencies from establishing, issuing, circulating or promoting a central bank digital currency (CBDC) within the United States and halts ongoing CBDC initiatives. It promotes the development of lawful and legitimate dollar-backed stablecoins worldwide to protect the sovereignty of the US dollar, calls for regulatory clarity based on well-defined jurisdictional boundaries, and protects access to banking services for digital-asset firms. A President's Working Group on Digital Asset Markets is established to propose a federal regulatory framework for digital assets, including stablecoins, and to evaluate a possible national digital asset stockpile. The order revokes Executive Order 14067 of 2022 and the Treasury's 'Framework for International Engagement on Digital Assets'. On the same day the SEC rescinded its Staff Accounting Bulletin 121 on crypto-asset custody.

implications: European supervisors gain direct oversight authority over critical ICT third-party providers, such as large cloud services, used by financial institutions.
Crypto-asset service providers are brought under the same digital operational resilience requirements as banks, insurers, and payment institutions.
Standard-setting bodies are developing supervisory frameworks for artificial intelligence and crypto-assets in financial services.
Traditional banks are being permitted to directly custody and serve digital-asset clients within the regulated perimeter.
transmission_channels: Direct supervision of shared ICT infrastructure can reduce common-point-of-failure risk but also concentrates regulatory responsibility and creates new supervisory dependencies.
Common standards reduce regulatory arbitrage and limit operational risk spillovers between crypto service providers and the broader financial system.
Model risk, operational failures, and asset-price volatility from automated decision-making and digital token markets.
Transmits digital-asset price volatility and operational risk directly onto bank balance sheets.
drivers: The EU Digital Operational Resilience Act enters into application and authorizes the European Supervisory Authorities to designate and directly supervise systemic technology providers.
DORA's scope explicitly includes crypto-asset service providers alongside traditional regulated financial entities.
Rapid adoption of AI and digital assets by financial institutions and markets.
Executive action protects banking access for digital-asset firms and rescinds restrictive crypto custody accounting guidance.
effects: The regulatory perimeter expands from regulated financial entities to their key digital infrastructure suppliers, subjecting concentrated technology providers to prudential oversight.
The regulatory treatment of digital asset firms converges with that of traditional finance regarding ICT risk management and resilience testing.
New prudential, conduct, and market-integrity requirements for digital finance.
Crypto-asset activities move from the regulatory periphery into the core banking sector.
modules.summary: The EU's Digital Operational Resilience Act now lets European supervisors directly oversee critical technology providers like cloud firms, while US executive action opens banking access to digital-asset firms. This brings crypto firms and tech suppliers inside the regulatory perimeter, so cloud outages or crypto price swings can pass straight onto bank balance sheets.

modules.name: Monetary Policy Stance and Transmission
modules.novelty_rationale: The shift from prolonged ultra-low or negative policy rates to positive and higher-for-longer regimes, including Japan ending monetary exceptionalism and reduced forward guidance, marks a structural break from the pre-pandemic baseline.
modules.reasoning: All implications describe central bank policy-rate decisions and their transmission to financial stability through bank profitability, funding costs, debt servicing, asset valuations, credit availability, and market liquidity. Although the directional stance varies across jurisdictions, the subsystem and transmission path are identical.

evidence_signals.title: Bank of Japan raises policy rate to 0.5%, the highest level since 2008
evidence_signals.content: At its Monetary Policy Meeting of 23–24 January 2025 the Bank of Japan decided, by an 8–1 majority vote, to raise its guideline for the uncollateralised overnight call rate from around 0.25% to around 0.5%, effective 27 January 2025; board member Toyoaki Nakamura dissented. It is the first hike since July 2024 and takes the policy rate to its highest level since 2008. In its quarterly Outlook Report the Board raised the median forecast for core CPI (all items less fresh food) to 2.7% for fiscal 2024, 2.4% for fiscal 2025 (from 1.9%) and 2.0% for fiscal 2026, citing higher import prices due to the weak yen and rising rice prices, while keeping real GDP growth forecasts at 1.1% and 1.0%. The Bank expects wages and prices to keep rising in a 'virtuous cycle', noted that global financial markets have been broadly stable, and stated that it will continue to raise the policy rate if the outlook is realised. Japan's December CPI, released the same day, rose 3.6% year on year. The yen strengthened by about 0.5% to around 155 per US dollar after the decision; higher Japanese rates are watched as a risk to yen-funded carry trades and as a factor for safe-haven flows into the Swiss franc.

evidence_signals.title: ECB January 2025 – Rate Cut -25bp, Deposit Rate 2.75%
evidence_signals.content: On 30 January 2025, the ECB Governing Council decided to lower the three key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. The deposit facility rate was reduced to 2.75%, the main refinancing operations rate to 2.90%, and the marginal lending facility rate to 3.15%, with effect from 5 February 2025. Rationale: The disinflation process is well on track. Inflation has continued to develop broadly in line with the December 2024 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area and is set to return to the Governing Council's 2% medium-term target in the course of 2025. Most measures of underlying inflation suggest that inflation will settle at around the target on a sustained basis. Domestic inflation remains high, mostly because wages and prices in certain sectors are still adjusting to the past inflation surge with a substantial delay. But wage growth is moderating as expected, and profits are partially buffering the impact on inflation. Annual inflation increased to 2.4% in December 2024, up from 2.2% in November; services inflation edged up to 4.0%. The Governing Council is determined to ensure that inflation stabilises sustainably at its 2% medium-term target. It will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance and is not pre-committing to a particular rate path.

evidence_signals.title: Fed FOMC January 2025 – Rates Held at 4.25-4.50% (Hawkish Hold)
evidence_signals.content: The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady at 4.25-4.50% at the January 28-29, 2025 FOMC meeting. This marks a pause in the rate-cutting cycle after 100 basis points of cuts in 2024 (Sep, Nov, Dec). Chair Powell stated the Fed is 'not in a hurry' to adjust policy. Solid labor market, inflation remains 'somewhat elevated'. Decision: unanimous 12-0.

evidence_signals.title: Swiss consumer prices fell 0.1% in December 2024; average annual inflation of 1.1% in 2024
evidence_signals.content: The Swiss Federal Statistical Office (FSO) reported on 7 January 2025 that the national consumer price index fell by 0.1% in December 2024 compared with the previous month, to 106.9 points (December 2020 = 100). Inflation was +0.6% compared with December 2023, after +0.7% in November. The decline in December was due to lower prices for package holidays abroad, medicines and various vegetables, while prices for hotel and supplementary accommodation rose. Food and non-alcoholic beverages were 0.9% cheaper and transport 1.9% cheaper than a year earlier. Average annual inflation reached +1.1% in 2024, after 2.1% in 2023 and 2.8% in 2022, with a high of 1.4% (April, May) and a low of 0.6% (October, December), well within the Swiss National Bank's definition of price stability (0–2%). Household electricity tariffs were cut by around 10% on average at the start of 2025, and the SNB's conditional forecast of December 2024 expects inflation of 0.3% for 2025.

implications: Central banks are ending prolonged periods of ultra-low or negative interest rates as inflation becomes entrenched.
Major central banks continue easing monetary policy as inflation converges back to target.
Major central banks maintain restrictive policy rates for extended periods as inflation remains sticky and labor markets stay solid.
Central banks adopt a more cautious easing cycle, delaying rate cuts until disinflation is firmly established.
Monetary policy is shifting toward a sustained easing bias as inflation forecasts fall well below target.
Central banks replace forward guidance with meeting-by-meeting, data-dependent rate decisions.
transmission_channels: Changes in policy rates affect bank profitability, government debt servicing costs, and the pricing of risk across financial markets.
Lower policy rates transmit through bank funding costs, lending rates, and asset prices, easing financial conditions and supporting credit growth.
Sustained elevated borrowing costs transmit through debt-servicing burdens, asset valuations, credit availability, and financial institution profitability.
Delayed policy easing prolongs tight financial conditions, affecting debt rollover, refinancing risk, and market liquidity.
Lower rates transmit through banking sector profitability, exchange rate pressures, and asset price valuations.
Reduced forward guidance increases uncertainty in bond markets and forward rates, affecting asset pricing and risk management.
drivers: Persistent inflation and wage-price dynamics in Japan after decades of price stability.
Sustained disinflation in the euro area with headline inflation approaching the 2% medium-term objective.
Persistent inflation above target combined with resilient employment reduces the urgency to ease monetary policy.
Inflation stickiness and strong labor markets make policymakers reluctant to cut rates preemptively.
Persistent disinflation and the central bank's conditional forecast of 0.3% inflation for 2025.
Deliberate policy strategy to maintain flexibility amid uncertain inflation and growth outlooks.
effects: Policy rates in Japan are moving from near-zero to positive territory, ending monetary exceptionalism.
Policy interest rates are lowered from restrictive levels, reducing the cost of borrowing across the economy.
A structural shift to a higher-for-longer interest rate regime, with policy rates remaining well above pre-pandemic lows for a prolonged period.
Longer policy lags and asymmetric monetary responses, where easing is slower and more conditional than tightening.
Policy rates remain low or are reduced, with limited scope or need for further tightening.
The future path of interest rates becomes less predictable to markets.
modules.summary: Central banks are diverging: the Bank of Japan raised rates to 0.5%, the highest since 2008, while the ECB is cutting and the Fed is holding at 4.25-4.50%, with less forward guidance. Rate moves flow through bank profits, government debt costs and asset prices, and less predictable paths unsettle bond markets and risk management.

modules.name: Bank capital regulation framework
modules.novelty_rationale: Builds on established post-crisis Basel frameworks but combines simultaneous national implementation, supervisory deregulation in the United States, and structural risk migration to non-bank financial institutions.
modules.reasoning: The implications describe one prudential subsystem: bank capital and lending regulation. Drivers include Basel III transposition, risk retention rules, supervisory standards, and political shifts in oversight. The shared transmission path runs from capital requirements and underwriting standards to bank loss-absorbing capacity, risk-taking, credit supply, and risk migration to non-banks, ultimately shaping systemic vulnerability, contagion, and procyclicality.

evidence_signals.title: FSB: G20 Financial Regulatory Reforms Have Enhanced Securitisation Market Resilience
evidence_signals.content: The FSB published on 22 January 2025 the final evaluation of G20 securitisation reforms. Key findings: (1) IOSCO risk retention rules and Basel Committee prudential requirements have contributed to securitisation market resilience without material negative side-effects on financing to the economy. (2) Complex GFC-era structures (subprime securitisations, CDOs, re-securitisations) have declined significantly; market is more transparent. (3) Warning: The post-GFC securitisation market has not yet been tested through a full credit cycle – particularly relevant for CLOs, which have grown significantly. (4) Risk redistribution: Reforms contributed to shift of risk from banks to NBFI sector; banks moving toward higher-rated tranches. (5) Issues for consideration: monitoring risks from synthetic risk transfers and private credit; effectiveness of risk retention for CLOs; implementation differences across FSB jurisdictions. Quote from Benjamin Weigert (Deutsche Bundesbank): 'The evaluation highlights the importance of the G20 reforms in enhancing securitisation market resilience. Nonetheless, recent market developments reinforce the need for authorities to monitor risks.' Ref: 3/2025.

evidence_signals.title: Fed's top bank supervisor Michael Barr to step down as Vice Chair for Supervision
evidence_signals.content: The Federal Reserve Board announced on 6 January 2025 that Michael S. Barr will step down as Vice Chair for Supervision effective 28 February 2025, or earlier if a successor is confirmed, while remaining a member of the Board of Governors, with a term running to January 2032. Barr, in office since July 2022, said that 'the risk of a dispute over the position could be a distraction from our mission'. He oversaw the review that attributed the 2023 failure of Silicon Valley Bank partly to weakened supervision, and proposed higher capital requirements for banks with more than USD 100 billion in assets under the US implementation of Basel III. His departure leaves the post open for the incoming administration, which favours bank deregulation; the Board does not intend to take up major rulemakings until a successor is confirmed, raising doubts about the future of the capital proposal. FDIC Chairman Martin Gruenberg also announced his departure for 19 January.

evidence_signals.title: Final Basel III standards enter into force in Switzerland on 1 January 2025
evidence_signals.content: On 1 January 2025 the final Basel III standards entered into force in Switzerland through the revised Capital Adequacy Ordinance (CAO) of the Federal Council and five new FINMA ordinances, which replace several FINMA circulars. The reform makes capital requirements more risk-sensitive: higher-risk business areas must be backed by more capital and lower-risk areas by less; the scope for internal models is restricted to achieve a transparent and internationally comparable calculation of capital, and requirements for credit risk, market risk and operational risk are revised. The Federal Council had confirmed in June 2024 that Switzerland would keep the 1 January 2025 start date despite delays in the implementation of the standards in the United States, the EU and the United Kingdom. The first reporting date under the new rules is 31 March 2025. The national implementation began before the takeover of Credit Suisse by UBS in March 2023 and is separate from the ongoing too-big-to-fail review.

evidence_signals.title: Stricter capital and self-regulation rules for mortgage lending take effect in Switzerland
evidence_signals.content: Together with the final Basel III standards, new rules for mortgage financing took effect in Switzerland on 1 January 2025. FINMA recognises the adjusted self-regulation of the Swiss Bankers Association on mortgage lending as a binding minimum standard; the guidelines revise minimum requirements for own funds and amortisation as well as qualitative requirements. In line with Basel III, risk weights are now differentiated by loan-to-value ratio for both owner-occupied and investment properties, and the risk weights for higher loan-to-value investment ('buy-to-let') properties are significantly higher than before. FINMA has repeatedly described the risks of overheating in the Swiss residential real estate market as high and pays close attention to institutions heavily exposed to investment properties; it announced that it will monitor the application of the new minimum standards and take measures at individual institutions where needed. Falling mortgage rates after the SNB's rate cuts in 2024 are supporting demand for residential property.

implications: Post-crisis regulatory reforms have structurally simplified securitisation markets and reduced their opacity.
Securitisation risk is structurally migrating from banks to non-bank financial institutions.
US banking supervision is shifting toward deregulation as a new political administration takes office, casting doubt on stricter capital rules for large banks.
Final Basel III capital standards are transposed into national law, making bank capital requirements more risk-sensitive and limiting reliance on internal models.
General capital adequacy reform proceeds on a separate regulatory track from too-big-to-fail requirements for systemically important banks.
Regulators impose higher, risk-sensitive capital requirements on mortgage lending, especially for high loan-to-value investment properties, to limit real estate risk accumulation.
Authorities convert industry self-regulatory guidelines on mortgage lending into binding minimum supervisory standards applicable to all institutions.
A major financial center adopts the final Basel III standards on schedule while other large jurisdictions delay implementation.
transmission_channels: Simpler and more transparent securitisation structures reduce information asymmetry and contagion potential, lowering the likelihood of a securitisation-triggered systemic event.
Risk concentration in less-regulated NBFIs can transmit losses to the banking system through direct exposures, funding linkages, and market-wide valuation spillovers during a downturn.
Reduced capital requirements and supervisory oversight weaken the loss-absorbing capacity and risk management of large banks, increasing systemic vulnerability
Changes in capital charges alter the relative cost of different banking activities, affecting risk-taking, credit supply, and the loss-absorbing capacity of the banking sector.
Higher cumulative capital requirements for systemically important banks reduce leverage and failure risk but can affect profitability, market structure, and resolvability.
Higher capital requirements increase loss-absorbing capacity and reduce credit procyclicality, limiting the transmission of housing price corrections to bank balance sheets.
Uniform binding standards limit regulatory arbitrage and ensure consistent risk management across banks, reducing the risk of a race to the bottom in lending criteria.
Temporary regulatory asymmetry can affect cross-border competitiveness, the location of banking activities, and incentives for regulatory arbitrage.
drivers: Implementation of G20-endorsed IOSCO risk retention rules and Basel Committee prudential capital requirements.
Higher regulatory capital and risk-retention requirements making bank holding of securitisation exposures less attractive.
Incoming administration's stated preference for bank deregulation and control over regulatory leadership appointments
Implementation of internationally agreed Basel III reforms through revised national capital adequacy regulations.
Distinct policy workstreams for baseline Basel III implementation and jurisdiction-specific rules for globally systemically important institutions.
Supervisory concern about overheating in residential real estate markets and implementation of final Basel III standards.
Regulatory objective to eliminate inconsistent application of lending standards and address systemic real estate risk.
A national decision to maintain the original implementation date despite delays in the United States, European Union, and United Kingdom.
effects: Complex pre-crisis structures such as subprime securitisations, CDOs, and re-securitisations have declined, while market transparency has increased without materially reducing financing to the economy.
Banks concentrate in higher-rated tranches while NBFIs absorb a larger share of lower-rated and more complex securitisation risk, including CLOs and synthetic risk transfers.
Suspension of major rulemakings, including the Basel III endgame capital proposal, and a likely loosening of supervisory standards for banks above USD 100 billion in assets
Risk-weighted assets are calculated more uniformly, with higher capital backing for riskier activities and lower capital for safer ones.
The largest banks become subject to layered capital requirements from both the new general framework and separate systemic overlays.
Banks must hold more capital against riskier mortgage exposures, constraining lending to high-LTV buy-to-let segments and reducing leverage in the housing market.
Mortgage underwriting rules become enforceable minimum requirements, ending reliance on voluntary industry compliance and reducing competitive underwriting.
Banks in the adopting jurisdiction face the new capital regime earlier than competitors in other major financial centers.
modules.summary: Final Basel III capital rules take effect in Switzerland on schedule, while the United States suspends its endgame proposal and shifts toward lighter bank supervision under the incoming administration. Diverging rules could shift risky lending and securitisation to non-banks or looser jurisdictions, leaving the banking system less able to absorb losses in a downturn.

modules.name: Climate financial risk surveillance
modules.novelty_rationale: Climate risk has moved from peripheral central bank innovation to embedded prudential surveillance and macroprudential policy, while physical climate baselines are shifting faster than risk models can recalibrate.
modules.reasoning: The implications describe one subsystem in which climate physical and transition risks transmit to financial stability through asset repricing, collateral devaluation, insurance protection gaps, and insurer capital erosion. Implications one to three show authorities institutionalizing climate risk tools and macroprudential responses; implications four to nine show physical risks crystallizing through real estate, insurance, and reinsurance channels into bank and sovereign balance sheets.

evidence_signals.title: BIS Innovation Hub sets out 2025–26 work programme: AI-enabled supervision and green finance
evidence_signals.content: On 14 January 2025 the Bank for International Settlements published the 2025–26 work programme of its Innovation Hub. At the start of 2025 the Hub's portfolio comprised 26 active projects, with 31 projects completed since its establishment in 2019 and 16 new projects started in 2024. The first two new projects of 2025 will develop AI-enabled tools, one to support financial regulation and supervision (suptech) and one for green finance. The Hub's ongoing work on tokenisation and next-generation financial market infrastructure includes the Project Agorá initiative with seven central banks and more than 40 private financial firms exploring tokenised correspondent banking for cross-border payments, and aims to exploit synergies across the existing project portfolio. The Hub serves as a focal point for a network of central bank innovation experts; its Swiss Centre is hosted in Zurich in cooperation with the Swiss National Bank.

evidence_signals.title: FSB Work Programme for 2025
evidence_signals.content: The FSB published its Work Programme for 2025 on 23 January 2025, outlining key regulatory and financial stability priorities for the year. Priority areas: (1) Supporting global cooperation on financial stability; (2) Enhancing resilience of non-bank financial intermediation (NBFI) while preserving its benefits – major G20 deliverable; (3) Harnessing benefits of digital innovation (crypto-assets, AI in finance, cross-border payments) while containing risks – major G20 deliverable; (4) Implementing the systemically important financial institution (SIFI) framework; (5) Addressing financial risks from climate change – climate roadmap progress; (6) Enhancing cross-border payments; (7) Completing resolution reforms. Key G20 deliverables planned: NBFI leverage policy recommendations (Jul 2025); Vulnerabilities from AI in finance (Oct 2025); Thematic peer review on crypto-assets (Oct 2025); FSB Annual Report (Dec 2025). Context: FSB is chaired by Klaas Knot (DNB). Secretariat in Basel, hosted by BIS.

evidence_signals.title: FSB: Analytical Framework and Toolkit to Assess Climate-Related Vulnerabilities
evidence_signals.content: The FSB published on 16 January 2025 a new analytical framework and toolkit to assess climate-related vulnerabilities in the global financial system. Key elements: (1) Framework traces how physical and transition climate risks transmit and amplify within the global financial system, building on the FSB Financial Stability Surveillance Framework. (2) Three categories of forward-looking toolkit metrics: proxies (early signals on drivers of transition/physical risks); exposure metrics (direct and indirect exposures in real economy and financial system); risk metrics (quantify impacts for financial institutions). (3) Case study: crystallisation of physical climate risks via real estate markets and changes in insurance coverage. Quotes: 'The framework provides a forward-looking approach to capture the unique aspects of climate risks while staying rooted in traditional financial stability analysis' (Sarah Breeden, Bank of England Deputy Governor). Policy area: Climate-related Risks. Ref: 2/2025. Part of FSB Roadmap to Address Climate-related Financial Risks (G20 mandate, July 2021).

evidence_signals.title: Confirmed: 2024 was the hottest year on record, says UN weather agency
evidence_signals.content: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) confirmed on 10 January 2025 that 2024 was the warmest year on record, based on six international datasets. The global average surface temperature was 1.55 °C (±0.13 °C) above the 1850–1900 average, which means the world has likely experienced the first calendar year more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels. The past ten years, 2015–2024, are the ten warmest on record, and ocean heat content reached a new record. 'Climate history is playing out before our eyes', said WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo, citing devastating extreme weather, rising sea levels and melting ice. WMO stressed that a single year above 1.5 °C does not mean that the long-term Paris Agreement goal, measured over decades, has been missed, but that every fraction of a degree of warming increases impacts on lives, economies and the planet. UN Secretary-General António Guterres called on governments to deliver new national climate action plans in 2025.

evidence_signals.title: Munich Re: natural disasters caused USD 140 billion of insured losses in 2024 as Los Angeles wildfires start 2025
evidence_signals.content: According to the reinsurer Munich Re's annual natural catastrophe report of 9 January 2025, natural disasters caused overall losses of USD 320 billion in 2024 (2023: USD 268 billion), of which USD 140 billion were insured – the third-highest insured total since 1980, the highest since 2017 and almost 50% above the ten-year average. Weather-related events accounted for 93% of overall and 97% of insured losses; hurricanes Helene and Milton in the United States were the costliest events, and 'non-peak' perils such as floods, wildfires and severe thunderstorms caused USD 136 billion of losses, about USD 67 billion of them insured. About 11,000 people died in natural disasters. 'Climate change is showing its claws', Munich Re said. The report was published as wildfires were destroying large parts of Los Angeles, threatening to become the costliest wildfire on record; California prohibited insurers from cancelling or not renewing home policies in the affected areas. With mounting claims, the cost of reinsurance is rising.

implications: Central banks are integrating green finance into their innovation and operational agendas.
Financial stability authorities are embedding climate-related physical and transition risks into macroprudential policy and supervision.
Climate-related risk assessment is being institutionalized within standard financial stability surveillance frameworks.
Physical climate risks are crystallizing through real estate markets and shifts in insurance coverage, creating transmission channels to financial stability.
Global temperatures have crossed the 1.5 °C annual threshold, marking a structural shift in the climate system.
Acute and chronic physical climate risks are intensifying as global temperatures and ocean heat content rise.
Climate change is increasing the frequency and severity of weather-related natural catastrophes, driving structurally higher insured losses and reinsurance costs.
Authorities are restricting insurers from cancelling or non-renewing policies in disaster-affected areas, constraining risk-based underwriting.
The gap between overall and insured catastrophe losses is widening as coverage becomes costlier and less available.
transmission_channels: Climate-related risk assessment tools and data standards influence prudential supervision and financial stability monitoring
Repricing of carbon-exposed assets and credit deterioration among borrowers facing physical or transition risks.
Climate risks propagate via real estate valuations, insurance coverage changes, and direct and indirect exposures across financial institutions.
Reduced collateral values and credit losses from climate-exposed real estate and insurance-linked exposures affect lending and solvency.
Reduced reliability of climate risk models leads to mispricing of exposed assets and insurance underwriting.
Direct damage to property and infrastructure, business interruption, and higher insurance claims transmit losses to financial institutions.

Higher claims erode insurer and reinsurer capital, leading to increased premiums, reduced coverage availability, and potential solvency stress that transmits to banks via corporate and household balance sheets
Artificially suppressed premiums weaken insurer capital buffers and may shift risk to state-backed insurers of last resort or to banks holding exposed mortgage collateral
drivers: Climate transition pressures and sustainability-related mandates
Increasing climate-related physical events and the economic transition to a low-carbon economy.
G20 mandate and the FSB climate roadmap, combined with growing evidence that physical and transition risks transmit through the financial system.
Increasing frequency and severity of climate-related physical events.
Continued accumulation of greenhouse gases and ocean heat uptake.
Rising global average temperatures, record ocean heat, and melting ice.
Rising global temperatures and atmospheric volatility intensifying weather extremes
Insurer withdrawals and non-renewals amid mounting climate-related claims in exposed regions
effects: Environmental finance tools and data become incorporated into central bank innovation portfolios and risk frameworks
Climate risk factors incorporated into financial stability assessments and supervisory expectations.
Standardized, forward-looking analytical tools and metrics are embedded in global financial stability monitoring.
Property devaluation and insurance protection gaps transmit climate losses to financial institution balance sheets.
Historical climate baselines no longer reliably predict future physical conditions.
More frequent and severe extreme weather events, sea-level rise, and environmental degradation.
A persistent step-up in weather-related insured losses and reinsurance pricing
Regulatory limits on underwriting freedom and risk pricing in catastrophe-prone markets
modules.summary: Central banks and the Financial Stability Board are embedding climate risks into supervision and macroprudential policy, after 2024 became the hottest year on record and insured disaster losses hit USD 140 billion. Floods and wildfires can cut property values and shrink insurance coverage, eroding the collateral behind bank loans and straining insurer capital.

modules.name: Central bank balance sheet and reserve management
modules.novelty_rationale: Central bank reserve revaluation affecting fiscal transfers is established, but the scale of recent profits and the explicit integration of FX intervention with rate setting mark a recent evolution in monetary-fiscal transmission.
modules.reasoning: Implications 2, 3, and 4 describe a subsystem in which central bank balance sheet operations—foreign exchange intervention and mark-to-market valuation of reserves—directly determine distributable profits and capital, creating a fiscal-monetary linkage to government budgets. Implication 1 concerns forward guidance and interest rate predictability transmitted through bond markets, a different channel, and is therefore excluded.

evidence_signals.title: SNB data portal: EUR/CHF monthly average of 0.9416 in January 2025
evidence_signals.content: According to the Swiss National Bank's data portal (cube 'devkum', monthly averages of foreign exchange rates, 11:00 fixing), the euro traded at an average of 0.94162 Swiss francs in January 2025. The franc thus remained close to its strongest levels against the euro, after the SNB had cut its policy rate by 50 basis points to 0.5% in December 2024 and stated that it remains willing to intervene in the foreign exchange market as necessary. The EUR/CHF rate is a key transmission channel for imported inflation in Switzerland and a central reference variable for the SNB's monetary policy.

evidence_signals.title: SNB expects record annual profit of around CHF 80 billion for 2024, resumes distribution to Confederation and cantons
evidence_signals.content: According to provisional calculations published on 9 January 2025, the Swiss National Bank will report a profit of around CHF 80 billion for 2024, after a loss of CHF 3.2 billion in 2023 and well above the previous record of CHF 54.4 billion in 2017. The result consists of a profit of around CHF 67 billion on foreign currency positions, a valuation gain of CHF 21.2 billion on gold holdings and a loss of CHF 7.4 billion on Swiss franc positions; the foreign currency result benefited from rising equity markets, a stronger US dollar and a higher gold price. After an allocation of CHF 11.6 billion to the provisions for currency reserves and taking into account the negative distribution reserve of CHF 53.2 billion, the net profit amounts to about CHF 16 billion. This allows the legal maximum dividend of CHF 15 per share and a distribution of CHF 3 billion to the Confederation (one third) and the cantons (two thirds), after two years without a distribution. The SNB's result depends heavily on exchange rates and financial market developments and is therefore very volatile.

implications: Monetary policy frameworks pair interest-rate adjustments with explicit readiness to intervene directly in foreign-exchange markets.
Central bank balance sheet revaluation gains and losses are a structurally significant and volatile source of public sector revenue.
Central bank profitability is increasingly driven by global financial asset valuation rather than interest rate differentials.
transmission_channels: Direct FX market intervention altering currency supply and demand while signaling future policy actions, transmitting to asset valuations and capital flows.
Central bank profits are transferred to the treasury and subnational governments; valuation losses reduce or suspend distributions, affecting fiscal planning and debt sustainability.
Mark-to-market gains on reserves boost distributable profits; market corrections generate losses that can erode central bank capital and eliminate profit transfers.
drivers: Central banks signaling willingness to conduct FX operations alongside policy rate changes to manage currency strength.
Large foreign exchange and gold reserves held by central banks, marked to market through the profit and loss account.
The composition of central bank balance sheets (foreign currency, gold, and equity exposures) and global financial market cycles.
effects: Greater blending of conventional interest-rate policy with direct exchange-rate management, shifting market expectations of central bank responses.
Government budgets are directly exposed to central bank financial market performance, creating a fiscal-monetary linkage where public revenue fluctuates with asset prices and exchange rates.
Central bank income is pro-cyclical with financial markets and less tied to monetary policy operations, making it vulnerable to market downturns.
modules.summary: The Swiss National Bank now pairs rate decisions with direct currency intervention and expects a record CHF 80 billion profit for 2024, resuming payouts to the Confederation and cantons. Reserve gains and losses flow into government budgets, so market downturns could cut these transfers, strain fiscal planning and erode central bank capital.

modules.name: Conflict induced displacement and infrastructure shock
modules.novelty_rationale: Conflict-driven displacement and reconstruction financing are recurring phenomena, but simultaneous crises across multiple fragile states intensify the fiscal and capital-flow transmission to financial stability.
modules.reasoning: All implications describe armed conflict in fragile states generating displacement, infrastructure destruction, and fiscal pressures that transmit to financial stability through strained public finances, sovereign borrowing needs, risk premiums, capital flight, and disrupted trade and payment channels. Active conflict, refugee returns, and reconstruction gaps form a single conflict-to-fiscal-instability subsystem.

evidence_signals.title: 'Famine conditions are spreading' as Sudan's crisis worsens: Security Council
evidence_signals.content: Briefing the UN Security Council on 6 January 2025, OCHA's Edem Wosornu said that 'famine conditions are now present in five areas' of Sudan – the Zamzam, Al Salam and Abu Shouk camps for internally displaced people in North Darfur and the western Nuba Mountains. The latest analysis of the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) Famine Review Committee projects that famine will spread to five additional areas in North Darfur, including Um Kadadah and El Fasher, by May 2025, with 17 further areas at risk. After more than 20 months of war, over 11.5 million people are internally displaced and 3.2 million have fled to neighbouring countries; more than 24.6 million people, over half the population, face high levels of acute food insecurity. FAO Deputy Director-General Beth Bechdol warned that 'the stability of many nations in the region' is at risk. Sudan's government, which suspended its participation in the IPC system in December, contested the findings. The 2025 humanitarian response plan for Sudan requires USD 4.2 billion.

evidence_signals.title: Critical aid blocked in Gaza, as fuel shortages threaten lifesaving services
evidence_signals.content: Israeli authorities continue to deny UN-led efforts to reach North Gaza with lifesaving aid, including the most recent attempt on 10 January 2025, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported. Across the Gaza Strip, only 10 of 21 UN-planned humanitarian movements on the previous day were facilitated; seven were denied outright, three were impeded and one was cancelled for security and logistical reasons. OCHA is deeply concerned about dwindling fuel supplies: Palestinian telecommunication providers warned that their services may start to shut down because they lack fuel for generators, and the lack of fuel is crippling the health system and bakeries. Humanitarian partners in central Gaza have exhausted their warehouse stocks, while about 120,000 metric tonnes of food aid – enough for full rations for the whole population for more than three months – remain stuck outside the Strip. The hunger crisis continues to worsen amid supply shortages, access restrictions and violent armed looting.

evidence_signals.title: More than 125,000 refugees return to Syria in desperate conditions
evidence_signals.content: One month after the fall of the Assad government on 8 December 2024, UNHCR estimates that more than 125,000 Syrian refugees have returned to the country, mainly from Türkiye, Jordan and Lebanon, with Aleppo, Ar-Raqqa and Dar'a as the primary areas of return. Returnees arrive 'full of hope after years of exile', UN humanitarians said, but find destroyed housing, damaged infrastructure, a lack of basic services and a deteriorating economy, while winter conditions increase needs. Hundreds of thousands of people have also been newly displaced inside Syria since early December, primarily in Idleb and Aleppo governorates. UNHCR anticipates up to one million refugee returns between January and June 2025, alongside large numbers of internally displaced people going home, and stresses that sustainable return requires early recovery, reconstruction support and adequate funding of the humanitarian response.

implications: Prolonged armed conflict in a fragile state is driving mass internal displacement, cross-border refugee flows, and famine, destabilizing the surrounding region.
Prolonged high-intensity conflict in the Middle East is causing the systematic degradation of essential civilian infrastructure and basic services in affected areas.
Large-scale refugee and internally displaced person returns follow a political transition in a conflict-affected country.
Post-conflict reconstruction and early recovery create a structural financing gap in a devastated economy.
transmission_channels: Refugee inflows strain host-country public finances and social services; disrupted production and trade reduce regional output; security contagion raises risk premiums and triggers capital flight

Geopolitical instability transmits to financial stability through safe-haven capital flows, commodity price volatility, insurance and reinsurance exposures, and disruptions to regional trade and payment channels.
Displacement and return flows generate fiscal and social pressures in origin and host countries, affecting labor markets, housing demand, and public service delivery.
Reconstruction demands increase sovereign borrowing needs, draw on multilateral and bilateral aid, and affect macroeconomic stability through public investment and debt dynamics.
drivers: Ongoing civil war and erosion of state authority in Sudan
Sustained military operations and access restrictions imposed by parties to the conflict.
Regime change and improved perceived security conditions after the fall of the Assad government.
Extensive physical destruction of housing, infrastructure, and public services during prolonged conflict.
effects: Large-scale forced displacement, acute food insecurity, and heightened geopolitical risk in neighboring countries
Telecommunications, health, and food distribution systems are failing, increasing the risk of mass displacement, hunger, and regional destabilization.
Rapid population return to areas with destroyed housing, damaged infrastructure, and absent basic services.
Massive demand for reconstruction financing and public investment exceeding domestic fiscal capacity.
modules.summary: Wars in Sudan, Syria and Gaza are forcing millions from their homes while fighting and access restrictions destroy housing, telecoms and health services. Refugee flows strain neighbouring states' budgets, reconstruction needs raise sovereign borrowing, and higher risk premiums and capital flight can reach banks and markets.

modules.name: Swiss Franc Safe Haven Channel
modules.novelty_rationale: The Swiss franc's safe-haven status and pharmaceutical export dominance are long-standing structural features, but their interaction with monetary policy divergence, near-zero inflation, and shrinking trade diversification intensifies the transmission to financial stability.
modules.reasoning: Safe-haven capital inflows drive structural Swiss franc appreciation, which constrains monetary policy, suppresses imported inflation, and raises real debt burdens. Simultaneously, export earnings concentrate in chemicals and pharmaceuticals, narrowing the trade base and linking the current account and exchange rate to sector-specific shocks. Together these channels transmit external disturbances to bank balance sheets, credit exposures, and asset prices.

evidence_signals.title: Bank of Japan raises policy rate to 0.5%, the highest level since 2008
evidence_signals.content: At its Monetary Policy Meeting of 23–24 January 2025 the Bank of Japan decided, by an 8–1 majority vote, to raise its guideline for the uncollateralised overnight call rate from around 0.25% to around 0.5%, effective 27 January 2025; board member Toyoaki Nakamura dissented. It is the first hike since July 2024 and takes the policy rate to its highest level since 2008. In its quarterly Outlook Report the Board raised the median forecast for core CPI (all items less fresh food) to 2.7% for fiscal 2024, 2.4% for fiscal 2025 (from 1.9%) and 2.0% for fiscal 2026, citing higher import prices due to the weak yen and rising rice prices, while keeping real GDP growth forecasts at 1.1% and 1.0%. The Bank expects wages and prices to keep rising in a 'virtuous cycle', noted that global financial markets have been broadly stable, and stated that it will continue to raise the policy rate if the outlook is realised. Japan's December CPI, released the same day, rose 3.6% year on year. The yen strengthened by about 0.5% to around 155 per US dollar after the decision; higher Japanese rates are watched as a risk to yen-funded carry trades and as a factor for safe-haven flows into the Swiss franc.

evidence_signals.title: SNB data portal: EUR/CHF monthly average of 0.9416 in January 2025
evidence_signals.content: According to the Swiss National Bank's data portal (cube 'devkum', monthly averages of foreign exchange rates, 11:00 fixing), the euro traded at an average of 0.94162 Swiss francs in January 2025. The franc thus remained close to its strongest levels against the euro, after the SNB had cut its policy rate by 50 basis points to 0.5% in December 2024 and stated that it remains willing to intervene in the foreign exchange market as necessary. The EUR/CHF rate is a key transmission channel for imported inflation in Switzerland and a central reference variable for the SNB's monetary policy.

evidence_signals.title: Swiss consumer prices fell 0.1% in December 2024; average annual inflation of 1.1% in 2024
evidence_signals.content: The Swiss Federal Statistical Office (FSO) reported on 7 January 2025 that the national consumer price index fell by 0.1% in December 2024 compared with the previous month, to 106.9 points (December 2020 = 100). Inflation was +0.6% compared with December 2023, after +0.7% in November. The decline in December was due to lower prices for package holidays abroad, medicines and various vegetables, while prices for hotel and supplementary accommodation rose. Food and non-alcoholic beverages were 0.9% cheaper and transport 1.9% cheaper than a year earlier. Average annual inflation reached +1.1% in 2024, after 2.1% in 2023 and 2.8% in 2022, with a high of 1.4% (April, May) and a low of 0.6% (October, December), well within the Swiss National Bank's definition of price stability (0–2%). Household electricity tariffs were cut by around 10% on average at the start of 2025, and the SNB's conditional forecast of December 2024 expects inflation of 0.3% for 2025.

evidence_signals.title: Swiss foreign trade 2024: record exports driven almost entirely by chemicals and pharmaceuticals
evidence_signals.content: The Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS/BAZG) reported on 30 January 2025 that Swiss exports rose by 3.2% (real: +2.5%) to a record CHF 282.9 billion in 2024, after declines in both directions of trade in 2023. The record was achieved almost exclusively by the chemical-pharmaceutical sector, whose exports grew by 10.0% (medicines +7.7%) and which accounts for more than half of total exports; exports of chemical-pharmaceutical raw and basic materials doubled within a year. Most other product groups recorded falling foreign sales: watch exports declined by 2.8% and jewellery by 4.5% after record years. Imports fell by 1.6% to CHF 222.3 billion, with imports from Asia at their lowest level since 2020. The opposing trends resulted in a record trade surplus of CHF 60.6 billion. The concentration on a single sector makes Swiss exports sensitive to sector-specific trade policy measures such as tariffs on pharmaceuticals.

implications: Safe-haven demand for the Swiss franc rises during episodes of global monetary policy divergence and market stress.
A structurally strong Swiss franc persists against the euro despite domestic monetary easing, driven by safe-haven capital inflows.
Swiss inflation is structurally trending toward zero with repeated monthly consumer price declines.
Export earnings are becoming structurally concentrated in the chemical-pharmaceutical sector, eroding diversification across merchandise export categories.
Swiss foreign trade is losing diversification across product groups and partner markets as non-pharmaceutical exports and imports from Asia decline.
transmission_channels: Capital inflows into Swiss franc assets appreciate the currency and tighten domestic financial conditions.
The exchange-rate transmission channel of monetary policy, affecting imported inflation, export competitiveness, and domestic financial conditions.
Low inflation raises real debt burdens, compresses bank interest margins, and reduces nominal income growth.

Sector-specific trade policy measures, such as pharmaceutical tariffs, or demand shocks transmit directly to national export earnings, the current account surplus, and the Swiss franc exchange rate, affecting financial stability through trade-related credit exposures and banking sector profitability.

Reduced product and geographic diversification amplifies the transmission of sector-specific or region-specific disturbances to the trade balance and national income, increasing volatility in financial sector balance sheets and asset prices.
drivers: Higher Japanese rates and associated global market volatility boosting CHF attractiveness.
Persistent safe-haven demand for the Swiss franc amid euro-area economic and political uncertainty.
Normalization of global supply chains and imported price pressures, reinforced by a strong Swiss franc.
Sustained global demand and competitive advantage for Swiss pharmaceuticals and chemicals.
Weak demand for traditional Swiss export goods and reduced trade integration with Asian economies.
effects: Structural appreciation pressure on the Swiss franc complicates Swiss monetary conditions and export competitiveness.
Reduced effectiveness of interest-rate cuts in weakening the currency and persistent downward pressure on imported inflation.
Consumer price growth remains persistently near the lower bound of the central bank's price stability band.
A single sector accounts for the majority of total exports and determines the overall trade balance.
The external trade base narrows to fewer sectors and markets, concentrating risk.
modules.summary: Investors are buying Swiss francs as a safe haven, as Bank of Japan rate rises and euro-area uncertainty keep the franc strong despite Swiss rate cuts. This pushes Swiss inflation toward zero, squeezing bank margins and raising real debt burdens, while export earnings concentrate in pharmaceuticals, exposing banks to trade shocks.

modules.name: Geopolitical financial infrastructure risk
modules.novelty_rationale: Sanctions and cyber threats are not new, but their systemic application to core payment infrastructure and reserve assets marks a structural shift from the baseline of open financial connectivity.
modules.reasoning: Both implications describe geopolitical interference with the infrastructure underpinning cross-border finance: one through exclusion from messaging systems and immobilization of reserves, the other through state-backed cyber attacks on financial and communications systems. Both erode confidence in infrastructure neutrality and availability, prompting Swiss banks to adjust correspondent banking, collateral, liquidity buffers, and operational resilience, transmitting to financial stability through access and confidence channels.

evidence_signals.title: EU Council extends economic sanctions against Russia for six months, until 31 July 2025
evidence_signals.content: On 27 January 2025 the Council of the European Union renewed its economic restrictive measures against Russia for a further six months, until 31 July 2025. The sanctions, first introduced in 2014 and significantly expanded since February 2022, cover trade, finance, energy, technology, dual-use goods, industry, transport and luxury goods, including the ban on imports of seaborne crude oil and certain petroleum products, the exclusion of Russian banks from SWIFT and the immobilisation of Russian central bank assets of around EUR 210 billion. Renewal requires unanimity: Hungary had threatened for weeks to block the extension and lifted its objection after receiving a declaration on its energy security following the end of gas transit through Ukraine. Since February 2022 the EU has adopted 15 sanctions packages; a 16th package is being prepared for the third anniversary of the invasion on 24 February 2025. Switzerland, which aligns with EU sanctions, had added 54 individuals and 30 entities to its Russia list on 23 December 2024.

evidence_signals.title: OFAC sanctions Chinese firm linked to Salt Typhoon telecom hacks and hacker involved in US Treasury breach
evidence_signals.content: On 17 January 2025 the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned Yin Kecheng, a Shanghai-based cyber actor affiliated with China's Ministry of State Security, for his involvement in the recent compromise of the Treasury Department's Departmental Offices network, which Treasury had detected on 8 December 2024. OFAC also designated Sichuan Juxinhe Network Technology, a cybersecurity company with direct involvement in the Salt Typhoon group, which recently compromised the network infrastructure of multiple major US telecommunication and internet service providers, including AT&T and Verizon, to access private communications. Treasury described the intrusions as an example of an increasing number of PRC state-backed cyber activities that require costly remediation; the action follows the designation of Integrity Technology Group on 3 January for its role in the Flax Typhoon intrusions. All property of the designated persons in the United States is blocked.

implications: Access to global payment infrastructure and foreign exchange reserves is increasingly subject to geopolitical conditions.
State-backed cyber actors are increasingly targeting financial institutions and critical communications infrastructure as part of geopolitical competition.
transmission_channels: Perceived risks to fund accessibility and payment connectivity can prompt shifts in correspondent banking, collateral frameworks, and liquidity buffers at Swiss banks.
Direct disruption of financial operations, data breaches, and increased operational costs transmit to financial stability through operational resilience and confidence channels.
drivers: Exclusion of systemically important banks from messaging systems and immobilization of central bank assets.
State-sponsored cyber capabilities deployed by national intelligence services in great-power competition.
effects: Erosion of confidence in the neutrality and safety of global financial infrastructure and reserve assets.
Higher systemic cyber risk to the financial sector, requiring costly remediation and eroding confidence in critical infrastructure.
modules.summary: US and EU sanctions have cut Russian banks off from global payment messaging and frozen Russian central bank reserves, while state-backed hackers target banks and telecoms. Fear of losing access to payments and reserves can push Swiss banks to rewire correspondent banking and liquidity buffers, while cyber attacks disrupt operations and erode confidence.

modules.name: Tokenised payment and settlement infrastructure
modules.novelty_rationale: The displacement of central bank money and correspondent banking by tokenised private liabilities as the standard digital settlement layer is a structural reconfiguration without direct historical precedent.
modules.reasoning: All three implications describe the migration of payment and settlement activity onto tokenised digital rails. Implication 1 covers central bank-led tokenised infrastructure; implications 2 and 3 cover private stablecoins displacing CBDCs and intermediating reserve-currency demand. Together they show a shared transmission path: new settlement rails alter liquidity management, counterparty and redemption exposure, and cross-border financial transmission, while concentrating risk in a small set of private issuers.

evidence_signals.title: BIS Innovation Hub sets out 2025–26 work programme: AI-enabled supervision and green finance
evidence_signals.content: On 14 January 2025 the Bank for International Settlements published the 2025–26 work programme of its Innovation Hub. At the start of 2025 the Hub's portfolio comprised 26 active projects, with 31 projects completed since its establishment in 2019 and 16 new projects started in 2024. The first two new projects of 2025 will develop AI-enabled tools, one to support financial regulation and supervision (suptech) and one for green finance. The Hub's ongoing work on tokenisation and next-generation financial market infrastructure includes the Project Agorá initiative with seven central banks and more than 40 private financial firms exploring tokenised correspondent banking for cross-border payments, and aims to exploit synergies across the existing project portfolio. The Hub serves as a focal point for a network of central bank innovation experts; its Swiss Centre is hosted in Zurich in cooperation with the Swiss National Bank.

evidence_signals.title: US Executive Order 14178 'Strengthening American Leadership in Digital Financial Technology' prohibits a US CBDC
evidence_signals.content: On 23 January 2025 the US President signed Executive Order 14178, setting the policy of the new administration to 'support the responsible growth and use of digital assets, blockchain technology, and related technologies across all sectors of the economy'. The order prohibits agencies from establishing, issuing, circulating or promoting a central bank digital currency (CBDC) within the United States and halts ongoing CBDC initiatives. It promotes the development of lawful and legitimate dollar-backed stablecoins worldwide to protect the sovereignty of the US dollar, calls for regulatory clarity based on well-defined jurisdictional boundaries, and protects access to banking services for digital-asset firms. A President's Working Group on Digital Asset Markets is established to propose a federal regulatory framework for digital assets, including stablecoins, and to evaluate a possible national digital asset stockpile. The order revokes Executive Order 14067 of 2022 and the Treasury's 'Framework for International Engagement on Digital Assets'. On the same day the SEC rescinded its Staff Accounting Bulletin 121 on crypto-asset custody.

implications: Central banks are collaborating on tokenised infrastructure for cross-border payments and financial markets.
Major economies are opting for privately issued stablecoins over central bank digital currencies as the standard form of digital money.
The international role of a reserve currency is being maintained through private stablecoin networks rather than official digital currency initiatives.
transmission_channels: New settlement rails change liquidity management, counterparty exposure, and cross-border financial transmission channels
Introduces private issuer credit and redemption risk into payment and settlement chains that previously relied on central bank money.
Concentrates reserve-currency liquidity and redemption risk in a small number of private stablecoin issuers, creating spillover channels to global funding markets.
drivers: Distributed ledger technology and central bank efforts to modernize payment and settlement systems
A national government explicitly prohibits a central bank digital currency while promoting private dollar-backed stablecoins as the preferred digital monetary instrument.
A reserve-currency issuer promotes private stablecoins abroad to preserve currency sovereignty while rejecting a CBDC.
effects: Tokenised correspondent banking and next-generation financial market infrastructure become part of official cross-border payment architecture
The digital money supply shifts from central bank liabilities to private tokenized liabilities, reducing the public sector's direct role in digital payments.
Global demand for the reserve currency is intermediated by private issuers on blockchain networks instead of central bank or correspondent banking channels.
modules.summary: The United States has banned a central bank digital currency and promotes private dollar-backed stablecoins instead, while central banks collaborate on tokenised cross-border payment infrastructure. If private tokens replace central bank money in settlement, issuer credit and redemption risk enter payment chains, and a few stablecoin issuers could concentrate spillovers to global funding markets.

modules.name: Sticky Inflation and Monetary Policy
modules.novelty_rationale: The shift from cyclical disinflation to structurally sticky services inflation and higher term premiums is relatively new versus the low-inflation baseline, though wage-price pass-through mechanisms are well understood.
modules.reasoning: All implications trace a single transmission path: persistent inflation from wages, trade disruptions, or fiscal risk constrains monetary policy, keeping rates higher for longer; this raises debt-servicing costs across sovereign, corporate, and household sectors, erodes bank asset quality, and depresses long-dated asset valuations, forming one financial-stability subsystem.

evidence_signals.title: ECB January 2025 – Rate Cut -25bp, Deposit Rate 2.75%
evidence_signals.content: On 30 January 2025, the ECB Governing Council decided to lower the three key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. The deposit facility rate was reduced to 2.75%, the main refinancing operations rate to 2.90%, and the marginal lending facility rate to 3.15%, with effect from 5 February 2025. Rationale: The disinflation process is well on track. Inflation has continued to develop broadly in line with the December 2024 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area and is set to return to the Governing Council's 2% medium-term target in the course of 2025. Most measures of underlying inflation suggest that inflation will settle at around the target on a sustained basis. Domestic inflation remains high, mostly because wages and prices in certain sectors are still adjusting to the past inflation surge with a substantial delay. But wage growth is moderating as expected, and profits are partially buffering the impact on inflation. Annual inflation increased to 2.4% in December 2024, up from 2.2% in November; services inflation edged up to 4.0%. The Governing Council is determined to ensure that inflation stabilises sustainably at its 2% medium-term target. It will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance and is not pre-committing to a particular rate path.

evidence_signals.title: IMF WEO Update January 2025 – Global Growth 3.3%, US Upgraded, Trade Policy Risk
evidence_signals.content: IMF World Economic Outlook Update, January 2025: 'Global Growth: Divergent and Uncertain'. Published January 17, 2025. Global growth is projected at 3.3 percent both in 2025 and 2026, below the historical (2000–19) average of 3.7 percent. The forecast is broadly unchanged from the October 2024 WEO, primarily on account of an upward revision in the United States offsetting downward revisions in other major economies. Global headline inflation is expected to decline to 4.2 percent in 2025 and 3.5 percent in 2026, converging back to target earlier in advanced economies than in emerging market and developing economies. Medium-term risks to the baseline are tilted to the downside, while the near-term outlook is characterized by divergent risks. Upside risks could lift already-robust growth in the United States in the short run, whereas risks in other countries are on the downside amid elevated policy uncertainty. Policy-generated disruptions to the ongoing disinflation process could interrupt the pivot to easing monetary policy, with implications for fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Key risks: renewed inflationary pressures, trade policy uncertainty (US tariff proposals), geopolitical disruptions, abrupt shift in market sentiment. Country highlights: US growth revised up to 2.7% for 2025; euro area revised down to 1.0%; China growth 4.5%.

evidence_signals.title: ILO World Employment and Social Outlook: Trends 2025
evidence_signals.content: The ILO World Employment and Social Outlook (WESO) Trends 2025 report was published on January 16, 2025. Key findings: (1) Global unemployment rate held steady at 5.0% in 2024, with employment growth in line with labour force growth. However, youth unemployment remained high at 12.6%, with little improvement. (2) Global jobs gap reached 402 million in 2024: 186 million unemployed, 137 million temporarily unavailable to work, 79 million discouraged workers. (3) NEET rates (Not in Education, Employment or Training): 85.8 million young men (13.1%) and 173.3 million young women (28.2%) were NEET globally in 2024, up by 1 million and 1.8 million respectively from 2023. In low-income countries: young men 15.8 million (20.4%), young women 28.2 million (37.0%). (4) Informal work and working poverty returned to pre-pandemic levels; real wages only increased in some advanced economies. (5) Economic growth: 3.2% in 2024, down from 3.3% in 2023 and 3.6% in 2022. Similar growth expected in 2025, with gradual deceleration over medium term. (6) Labour force participation declined in low-income countries, increased in high-income nations (mainly older workers and women). Gender gaps remain wide. (7) Opportunities: Renewable energy jobs grew to 16.2 million worldwide (solar and hydrogen investment-driven); nearly half based in East Asia. Headline quote (ILO Director-General Gilbert F. Houngbo): 'Decent work and productive employment are essential for achieving social justice and the Sustainable Development Goals. To avoid exacerbating already strained social cohesion, escalating climate impacts, and surging debt, we must act now to tackle labour market challenges and create a fairer, more sustainable future.' Key pressures: geopolitical tensions, rising costs of climate change, unresolved sovereign debt issues, persistent inflation eroding real wages.

evidence_signals.title: UK 30-year gilt yields rise to highest level since 1998 amid concerns over public finances
evidence_signals.content: UK long-term borrowing costs rose to their highest level in more than a quarter of a century in early January 2025. On 7 January the Debt Management Office auctioned GBP 2.25 billion of 30-year gilts at a yield of 5.198%, and the 30-year yield climbed to 5.37% on 8 January, the highest since 1998 and above the levels of the 2022 'mini-budget' crisis; the 10-year yield rose to around 4.8–4.9%, the highest since 2008. Sterling fell to about USD 1.22, its lowest since November 2023. The sell-off was part of a global rise in long-dated government bond yields led by US Treasuries, but was amplified by near-record UK debt issuance of about GBP 297 billion in the 2024–25 fiscal year, persistent inflation and economic stagnation. Analysts warned that higher interest costs could erase the GBP 9.9 billion of fiscal headroom left by the October budget, forcing Chancellor Rachel Reeves to cut spending or raise taxes again; the Treasury said the fiscal rules are 'non-negotiable'.

implications: Domestic wage and price adjustments keep services and core inflation sticky even as headline inflation falls.
Trade policy uncertainty and sticky inflation risk interrupting the disinflation process, delaying the pivot to monetary easing.
Real wage growth remains weak and informal work persists, leaving a large share of workers without income security despite moderate global growth.
Long-term sovereign bond yields are structurally repricing higher as investors demand larger term premiums for inflation and fiscal risk.
transmission_channels: Persistent services inflation maintains domestic price pressures, requiring a cautious, data-dependent policy stance and limiting rate cuts.
Prolonged restrictive borrowing costs increase debt-servicing pressure on sovereign, corporate, and household balance sheets.
Weaker household debt service capacity and higher consumer credit delinquencies transmit directly to bank asset quality.
Rising long-term yields lower asset valuations, mark down fixed-income portfolios, and increase economy-wide borrowing costs

Protectionist trade measures and policy-generated disruptions to price stability.
