modules.summary: As headline inflation falls, services prices and wages keep it above target, so the ECB cuts rates slowly and long-term bond yields are climbing, with UK 30-year gilts at their highest since 1998. Prolonged high borrowing costs strain government, business and household budgets, raising loan defaults and marking down bond portfolios banks hold.

modules.name: Cross-border cyber incident reporting
modules.novelty_rationale: National supervisory fragmentation is being replaced by harmonized EU-wide and FSB-aligned incident reporting and third-party dependency mapping, a structural shift away from jurisdiction-specific resilience oversight.
modules.reasoning: Both implications describe one transmission path: standardized cyber and ICT incident data plus third-party contract information flowing across borders, enabling supervisors to map shared technology exposures, detect contagion through common providers, and coordinate responses to limit systemic disruption.

evidence_signals.title: EU Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) applies from 17 January 2025
evidence_signals.content: From 17 January 2025, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 on digital operational resilience for the financial sector (DORA) and its technical standards apply across the EU, without a transitional period. DORA covers a wide range of financial entities, from credit and payment institutions to insurers, fund managers and crypto-asset service providers, and rests on five pillars: ICT risk management, classification and reporting of major ICT-related incidents, digital operational resilience testing including threat-led penetration testing, management of ICT third-party risk, and information sharing. Financial entities must be able to report major ICT incidents from day one and must submit registers of information on their contractual arrangements with ICT third-party providers, which competent authorities forward to the European Supervisory Authorities by 30 April 2025. On this basis the ESAs will designate critical ICT third-party providers, such as large cloud service providers, for direct EU oversight; the first designations are expected in the second half of 2025. In December 2024 the ESAs had urged entities to close remaining gaps, as several standards were finalised only late.

evidence_signals.title: FSB: Public Responses to Consultation on Format for Incident Reporting Exchange (FIRE)
evidence_signals.content: On 3 January 2025, the FSB published public consultation responses to the Format for Incident Reporting Exchange (FIRE) Consultation Report (Oct 2024). FIRE proposes a standardised format for reporting operational incidents, including cyber incidents, to financial authorities. The goal is to promote convergence and communication among financial supervisors and regulated firms, facilitating efficient incident response and recovery. Nine industry bodies submitted responses, including Bank Policy Institute, Deutsche Börse Group, Global Financial Markets Association, Institute of International Finance, and Global Legal Entity Identifier Foundation. Policy area: Cyber Resilience / Information Exchange.

implications: EU financial institutions must report major ICT incidents and disclose contractual arrangements with technology providers under a single harmonized framework.
Financial authorities are converging on standardized formats for cross-border cyber and operational incident reporting.
transmission_channels: Standardized incident and contract data allows authorities to map shared technology exposures and detect potential contagion through common providers.
Enables faster cross-border information sharing and coordinated response, limiting the transmission of cyber disruptions through the financial system.
drivers: Mandatory incident reporting and third-party risk register requirements apply immediately to a broad range of financial entities across the EU.
FSB-led effort to improve convergence and communication among supervisors and regulated firms for efficient incident response and recovery.
effects: National supervisory fragmentation over operational resilience is replaced by a cross-border EU-wide data flow on ICT incidents and dependencies.
Harmonized incident reporting requirements that reduce fragmentation across jurisdictions and institutions.
modules.summary: Under the EU's Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), effective January 2025, financial firms must report major cyber and technology incidents to supervisors, while the FSB develops a shared global reporting format. This lets supervisors see which banks rely on the same technology providers, so they can spot contagion early and coordinate before disruptions spread.

modules.name: Financial sanctions compliance perimeter
modules.novelty_rationale: Sanctions are expanding beyond traditional individual and entity designations to whole economic sectors, cyber actors, shipping vessels, and insurers, while being maintained as long-term geopolitical instruments rather than temporary tools.
modules.reasoning: All implications describe the same structural subsystem: the expansion and enforcement of international economic sanctions. They share a transmission path to financial stability through higher compliance costs, counterparty risk, de-risking, reduced access to dollar clearing, trade finance, and insurance, and persistent segmentation of cross-border financial relations along geopolitical blocs.

evidence_signals.title: OFAC sanctions Chinese firm linked to Salt Typhoon telecom hacks and hacker involved in US Treasury breach
evidence_signals.content: On 17 January 2025 the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned Yin Kecheng, a Shanghai-based cyber actor affiliated with China's Ministry of State Security, for his involvement in the recent compromise of the Treasury Department's Departmental Offices network, which Treasury had detected on 8 December 2024. OFAC also designated Sichuan Juxinhe Network Technology, a cybersecurity company with direct involvement in the Salt Typhoon group, which recently compromised the network infrastructure of multiple major US telecommunication and internet service providers, including AT&T and Verizon, to access private communications. Treasury described the intrusions as an example of an increasing number of PRC state-backed cyber activities that require costly remediation; the action follows the designation of Integrity Technology Group on 3 January for its role in the Flax Typhoon intrusions. All property of the designated persons in the United States is blocked.

evidence_signals.title: OFAC sanctions Gazprom Neft, Surgutneftegas and 183 vessels in sweeping action against Russia's oil sector
evidence_signals.content: On 10 January 2025 the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), in coordination with the US State Department and the UK, announced one of the largest sanctions actions against Russia's energy sector since 2022. OFAC designated the vertically integrated oil producers Gazprom Neft and Surgutneftegas together with more than two dozen of their subsidiaries, identified 183 oil-carrying vessels – many of them part of the 'shadow fleet' – as blocked property, and sanctioned oil traders, oilfield service providers, energy officials and the insurers Ingosstrakh and Alfastrakhovanie. A new determination under Executive Order 14024 authorises sanctions against any person operating in the energy sector of the Russian economy, and US persons will be prohibited from providing petroleum services to Russia from 27 February 2025. Treasury said the measures fulfil the G7 commitment to reduce Russian energy revenues and 'substantially increase the sanctions risks associated with the Russian oil trade', including shipping and financial facilitation. General licences allow the wind-down of transactions until 27 February 2025. The UK designated Gazprom Neft and Surgutneftegas on the same day.

evidence_signals.title: EU Council extends economic sanctions against Russia for six months, until 31 July 2025
evidence_signals.content: On 27 January 2025 the Council of the European Union renewed its economic restrictive measures against Russia for a further six months, until 31 July 2025. The sanctions, first introduced in 2014 and significantly expanded since February 2022, cover trade, finance, energy, technology, dual-use goods, industry, transport and luxury goods, including the ban on imports of seaborne crude oil and certain petroleum products, the exclusion of Russian banks from SWIFT and the immobilisation of Russian central bank assets of around EUR 210 billion. Renewal requires unanimity: Hungary had threatened for weeks to block the extension and lifted its objection after receiving a declaration on its energy security following the end of gas transit through Ukraine. Since February 2022 the EU has adopted 15 sanctions packages; a 16th package is being prepared for the third anniversary of the invasion on 24 February 2025. Switzerland, which aligns with EU sanctions, had added 54 individuals and 30 entities to its Russia list on 23 December 2024.

implications: Financial sanctions regimes are being expanded to designate cyber actors and entities involved in state-sponsored hacking.
Sanctions eligibility is being broadened to cover any person operating within an entire sector of a sanctioned economy.
Comprehensive economic sanctions against major economies are being maintained as a long-term instrument of geopolitical confrontation.
Sanctions enforcement is expanding to target the shipping vessels and insurers that facilitate energy exports from sanctioned states.
Major Western powers are coordinating sanctions on state-controlled energy producers to structurally cut a geopolitical rival's energy revenue.
transmission_channels: Asset freezes and restricted access to the US financial system increase compliance costs and counterparty risk for financial institutions.
Reduced access to dollar clearing, trade finance, and insurance for firms with business ties to the sanctioned sector.
Restrictions on trade finance, cross-border payments, and asset holdings increase compliance costs, counterparty risk, and operational complexity for Swiss financial institutions.
Higher shipping and insurance costs, increased risk of vessel blocking or seizure, and reduced access to traditional trade finance for sanctioned energy cargoes.
Disrupted benchmark pricing, shift to non-dollar settlement, and greater reliance on alternative financial infrastructure for sanctioned energy trade.
drivers: Use of OFAC and SDN designations as a national security countermeasure to cyber threats.
Executive determinations under sanctions authorities that designate whole economic sectors as sanctionable.
Sustained interstate conflict and strategic economic coercion by sanctioning blocs.
Coordinated Western efforts to reduce energy revenues from sanctioned states and increase risks in their oil trade.
G7 commitments to restrict energy export revenues from sanctioned states and enforce related price mechanisms.
effects: The sanctions perimeter now encompasses cyber activity, creating new compliance obligations and financial integrity risks.
Structural increase in extraterritorial compliance exposure and de-risking by global financial institutions and insurers.
Persistent segmentation of international trade, investment, and financial relations along geopolitical blocs.
Structural displacement of sanctioned energy shipments toward opaque, uninsured shadow fleets and non-Western insurance markets.
Structural fragmentation of global energy markets into separate Western and non-Western trading and financial blocs.
modules.summary: The US and its allies are widening financial sanctions from individuals to whole sectors, cyber hackers, ships and insurers, with OFAC recently designating Russia's oil firms and 183 vessels. This raises compliance costs and counterparty risk for banks, and can reduce access to dollar clearing, trade finance and insurance for firms tied to sanctioned business.

modules.name: Multilateral humanitarian access subsystem
modules.novelty_rationale: The humanitarian aid architecture is long-standing, but the deliberate suspension of independent multilateral monitoring and systematic obstruction of UN supply chains mark an intensification of politicization, while donor fiscal exposure remains a chronic structural feature.
modules.reasoning: All three implications describe components of the international humanitarian aid system—early-warning data, logistics and supply chains, and donor financing—whose disruption transmits to financial stability through delayed aid, deepening crises, cross-border spillovers, food and energy price volatility, fiscal pressure on donor governments, contingent liabilities, and risks to exposed logistics and insurance firms.

evidence_signals.title: 'Famine conditions are spreading' as Sudan's crisis worsens: Security Council
evidence_signals.content: Briefing the UN Security Council on 6 January 2025, OCHA's Edem Wosornu said that 'famine conditions are now present in five areas' of Sudan – the Zamzam, Al Salam and Abu Shouk camps for internally displaced people in North Darfur and the western Nuba Mountains. The latest analysis of the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) Famine Review Committee projects that famine will spread to five additional areas in North Darfur, including Um Kadadah and El Fasher, by May 2025, with 17 further areas at risk. After more than 20 months of war, over 11.5 million people are internally displaced and 3.2 million have fled to neighbouring countries; more than 24.6 million people, over half the population, face high levels of acute food insecurity. FAO Deputy Director-General Beth Bechdol warned that 'the stability of many nations in the region' is at risk. Sudan's government, which suspended its participation in the IPC system in December, contested the findings. The 2025 humanitarian response plan for Sudan requires USD 4.2 billion.

evidence_signals.title: Critical aid blocked in Gaza, as fuel shortages threaten lifesaving services
evidence_signals.content: Israeli authorities continue to deny UN-led efforts to reach North Gaza with lifesaving aid, including the most recent attempt on 10 January 2025, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported. Across the Gaza Strip, only 10 of 21 UN-planned humanitarian movements on the previous day were facilitated; seven were denied outright, three were impeded and one was cancelled for security and logistical reasons. OCHA is deeply concerned about dwindling fuel supplies: Palestinian telecommunication providers warned that their services may start to shut down because they lack fuel for generators, and the lack of fuel is crippling the health system and bakeries. Humanitarian partners in central Gaza have exhausted their warehouse stocks, while about 120,000 metric tonnes of food aid – enough for full rations for the whole population for more than three months – remain stuck outside the Strip. The hunger crisis continues to worsen amid supply shortages, access restrictions and violent armed looting.

evidence_signals.title: More than 125,000 refugees return to Syria in desperate conditions
evidence_signals.content: One month after the fall of the Assad government on 8 December 2024, UNHCR estimates that more than 125,000 Syrian refugees have returned to the country, mainly from Türkiye, Jordan and Lebanon, with Aleppo, Ar-Raqqa and Dar'a as the primary areas of return. Returnees arrive 'full of hope after years of exile', UN humanitarians said, but find destroyed housing, damaged infrastructure, a lack of basic services and a deteriorating economy, while winter conditions increase needs. Hundreds of thousands of people have also been newly displaced inside Syria since early December, primarily in Idleb and Aleppo governorates. UNHCR anticipates up to one million refugee returns between January and June 2025, alongside large numbers of internally displaced people going home, and stresses that sustainable return requires early recovery, reconstruction support and adequate funding of the humanitarian response.

implications: National governments are suspending participation in independent, multilateral early-warning and food-security monitoring systems.
Humanitarian supply chains in active conflict zones are being systematically blocked, preventing the delivery of food, fuel, and medical supplies.
Sustained international humanitarian aid requirements place pressure on donor burden-sharing and public finances.
transmission_channels: Lack of verified data slows donor decisions and aid disbursements, allowing crises to deepen and intensify cross-border spillovers

Supply chain disruption in conflict zones can amplify food and energy price volatility, increase fiscal pressure on donor governments, and create operational and reputational risks for logistics and insurance firms exposed to the region.
Humanitarian funding needs affect donor government budgets, create contingent fiscal liabilities, and influence macroeconomic stability through aid-dependent economies.
drivers: Political efforts to contest or suppress UN-verified humanitarian data by the Sudanese government
Denial and impediment of UN-led humanitarian movements by controlling authorities.
Projections of up to one million refugee returns and deteriorating economic conditions in the origin country.
effects: Weakening of independent crisis data and delayed international humanitarian response
Large volumes of pre-positioned aid remain stuck at borders, local stocks are exhausted, and aid-dependent populations face worsening crisis conditions.
Continued reliance on international humanitarian financing and coordinated donor responses for sustainable returns.
modules.summary: Sudan's government is contesting UN-verified hunger data, and aid convoys to conflict zones such as Gaza are being blocked, leaving food, fuel and medicine stuck at borders. This can push up food and energy prices, strain donor government budgets, and create losses for banks and insurers exposed to aid-dependent economies and regional logistics firms.

modules.name: Fiscal consolidation and debt sustainability
modules.novelty_rationale: Debt brakes and ageing-related spending are longstanding, but the simultaneous pressure from defence spending, sticky inflation, elevated sovereign issuance, and pension taxation changes marks a renewed structural fiscal tightening.
modules.reasoning: All three implications describe a single subsystem: fiscal consolidation under debt constraints. Implication 3 establishes the macro context of eroding fiscal headroom and rising sovereign borrowing costs; implications 1 and 2 detail the resulting consolidation measures—expenditure cuts, broader taxation, and pension withdrawal taxes—and their transmission through household disposable income, bank sovereign exposures, pension fund liquidity, and broader financial conditions.

evidence_signals.title: Swiss Federal Council opens consultation on 'relief package 27' to stabilise federal finances
evidence_signals.content: At its meeting on 29 January 2025 the Swiss Federal Council adopted the consultation draft of relief package 27 (RP27) and opened the consultation, which runs until 5 May 2025. The package of 59 measures is intended to reduce the federal budget by about CHF 2.7 billion in 2027 and CHF 3.6 billion in 2028, so that the debt brake can be respected despite rising expenditure for the armed forces and the old-age pension system (including the 13th AHV pension). More than half of the measures require amendments to federal law. The proposals include cuts of more than CHF 460 million per year in education, research and innovation, as well as higher taxation of capital withdrawals from the second and third pillars. Even with the package, federal expenditure is expected to grow by more than 2% per year in the medium term. Several parties and the cantons had already criticised the proposals in autumn 2024, so the package is expected to be politically contested.

evidence_signals.title: UK 30-year gilt yields rise to highest level since 1998 amid concerns over public finances
evidence_signals.content: UK long-term borrowing costs rose to their highest level in more than a quarter of a century in early January 2025. On 7 January the Debt Management Office auctioned GBP 2.25 billion of 30-year gilts at a yield of 5.198%, and the 30-year yield climbed to 5.37% on 8 January, the highest since 1998 and above the levels of the 2022 'mini-budget' crisis; the 10-year yield rose to around 4.8–4.9%, the highest since 2008. Sterling fell to about USD 1.22, its lowest since November 2023. The sell-off was part of a global rise in long-dated government bond yields led by US Treasuries, but was amplified by near-record UK debt issuance of about GBP 297 billion in the 2024–25 fiscal year, persistent inflation and economic stagnation. Analysts warned that higher interest costs could erase the GBP 9.9 billion of fiscal headroom left by the October budget, forcing Chancellor Rachel Reeves to cut spending or raise taxes again; the Treasury said the fiscal rules are 'non-negotiable'.

implications: National governments implement structural fiscal consolidation—cutting expenditure and raising taxes—to remain within constitutional debt brakes while mandatory spending on defence and ageing-related pensions rises.
Policymakers raise taxes on lump-sum withdrawals from occupational and private pension schemes as part of fiscal consolidation, structurally changing the taxation of retirement savings.
Elevated sovereign debt issuance and persistent inflation are eroding fiscal headroom and pushing long-term government borrowing costs higher in advanced economies.
transmission_channels: Reduced public spending and higher taxation lower household and corporate disposable income and aggregate demand, affect regional government budgets and sovereign debt issuance, and can alter bank exposures to the public sector and the perceived creditworthiness of the state.

Smaller after-tax pension withdrawals reduce household wealth available for consumption and housing finance, affect pension fund and retirement-account liquidity, and can influence occupational and private pension asset allocation and related bank and insurer balance sheets.
Higher debt-service costs crowd out public expenditure and transmit sovereign stress to bank balance sheets and broader financial conditions
drivers: Legislated growth in non-discretionary spending for defence and old-age pensions (including additional pension benefits) together with a constitutional debt brake that constrains deficit financing.
The need to generate additional revenue to respect the debt brake, applied to occupational and private pension capital withdrawals.
Large-scale government borrowing amid sticky inflation and stagnant growth
effects: A durably tighter fiscal stance with lower deficits and a broader tax base, even as total public expenditure continues to grow at a moderate medium-term pace.
A lasting shift in pension taxation that lowers the after-tax value of retirement lump sums and modifies household saving, drawdown, and housing-financing incentives.
Reduced fiscal space forces spending cuts or tax increases to maintain market confidence
modules.summary: Governments are cutting spending and raising taxes—including levies on pension lump-sum withdrawals—to meet constitutional debt brakes as defence and pension costs climb, and heavy borrowing pushes long-term yields up. Lower household and corporate income and smaller pension withdrawals curb spending, while higher debt-service costs can pass sovereign stress to bank balance sheets.

modules.name: Equity Market Risk Compression
modules.novelty_rationale: Volatility suppression through options selling and passive flows is an established structural feature, but the layering of AI-driven mega-cap concentration and rapid repricing from low-cost frontier models creates a novel transmission pathway for idiosyncratic shocks to become systemic.
modules.reasoning: The implications jointly describe an equity market subsystem in which suppressed implied volatility and muted political sensitivity underprice tail risk, while concentration in a narrow set of technology equities and passive index mechanics amplify single-stock shocks into broad market moves. AI cost breakthroughs can trigger abrupt repricing of these concentrated positions. Stress transmits via leverage, margin calls, dealer gamma hedging, index-tracking forced selling, and collateral erosion into credit, funding, and banking sectors.

evidence_signals.title: CBOE VIX volatility index: January 2025 monthly average of 16.76 (range 14.85–19.54)
evidence_signals.content: According to the CBOE VIX daily history, the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX), which measures expected 30-day volatility of the S&P 500, closed at an average of 16.76 in January 2025, within a range of 14.85 to 19.54 over 22 trading days. Implied equity volatility thus stayed close to its long-term median despite the change of US administration and announcements on tariffs; readings above 30 are usually associated with market stress.

evidence_signals.title: DeepSeek shock: Nvidia loses about USD 590 billion in market value in record one-day drop
evidence_signals.content: On 27 January 2025 global technology stocks sold off after the Chinese start-up DeepSeek showed that its AI models can match leading US models at a fraction of the cost. Nvidia shares fell almost 17%, erasing about USD 589 billion of market capitalisation, the largest one-day loss of market value for any company in US stock market history and more than double Nvidia's previous record from September 2024. Broadcom fell 17%, TSMC 13%, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 3.1% while the S&P 500 fell 1.5%. DeepSeek-V3, launched on 10 January, was reportedly trained on Nvidia's lower-capability H800 chips for less than USD 6 million, and DeepSeek-R1, released the previous week, is reportedly 20 to 50 times cheaper to use than OpenAI's comparable model. Before the sell-off Nvidia traded at nearly 60 times earnings, compared with 22 for the S&P 500; the sell-off raised questions about the valuations and the very large AI investment plans of US technology firms.

implications: US equity implied volatility remains compressed near long-term medians even during periods of elevated political and trade-policy uncertainty.
Equity markets are becoming structurally less responsive to political transitions and tariff announcements, weakening volatility as a real-time risk indicator.
Mega-cap technology concentration increases the transmission of single-stock shocks to broad market indices.
Low-cost frontier AI models prompt rapid repricing of high-valuation technology equities and their suppliers.
transmission_channels: Suppressed volatility encourages leverage and risk concentration; volatility spikes trigger margin calls and options dealer hedging that transmit stress rapidly to credit and funding markets.
Underpriced political risk means shocks arrive unhedged, causing sharper corrections and spillovers into banking sector credit and corporate funding markets.
Forced selling by index funds and leveraged investors, margin-related liquidations, and confidence spillovers to other risk assets.
Mark-to-market losses on concentrated equity positions, reduced collateral values, and volatility transmission through index-tracking and leveraged portfolios.
drivers: Structural growth in options-based volatility selling and dealer gamma hedging, alongside passive investment flows that dampen price swings.
Repeated experience that political shocks have not caused sustained market declines, combined with strong liquidity and expectations of official backstops.
Persistent investor crowding into a narrow set of AI-linked equities and passive index weighting mechanisms.
Algorithmic breakthroughs that deliver comparable AI performance using significantly less compute and capital.
effects: Tail risk in equity markets is systematically underpriced, raising the likelihood of abrupt volatility spikes and forced deleveraging when a shock finally occurs.
Political and geopolitical risks are underweighted in asset prices, reducing the early-warning value of equity volatility for financial stability monitoring.
Greater systemic sensitivity of broad equity benchmarks to idiosyncratic price movements in a few dominant firms.
Lower expected profitability and compressed valuation multiples for AI hardware incumbents, with spillover to technology-heavy indices.
modules.summary: US equity volatility, tracked by the VIX, sits near long-term medians despite political and trade shocks, as options selling and passive funds calm prices while AI mega-caps like Nvidia dominate indices. A shock could trigger margin calls and dealer hedging, forcing sales that spread stress into bank credit and corporate funding markets.

evidence_signals.title: Bank of Japan raises policy rate to 0.5%, the highest level since 2008
evidence_signals.content: At its Monetary Policy Meeting of 23–24 January 2025 the Bank of Japan decided, by an 8–1 majority vote, to raise its guideline for the uncollateralised overnight call rate from around 0.25% to around 0.5%, effective 27 January 2025; board member Toyoaki Nakamura dissented. It is the first hike since July 2024 and takes the policy rate to its highest level since 2008. In its quarterly Outlook Report the Board raised the median forecast for core CPI (all items less fresh food) to 2.7% for fiscal 2024, 2.4% for fiscal 2025 (from 1.9%) and 2.0% for fiscal 2026, citing higher import prices due to the weak yen and rising rice prices, while keeping real GDP growth forecasts at 1.1% and 1.0%. The Bank expects wages and prices to keep rising in a 'virtuous cycle', noted that global financial markets have been broadly stable, and stated that it will continue to raise the policy rate if the outlook is realised. Japan's December CPI, released the same day, rose 3.6% year on year. The yen strengthened by about 0.5% to around 155 per US dollar after the decision; higher Japanese rates are watched as a risk to yen-funded carry trades and as a factor for safe-haven flows into the Swiss franc.

Global growth is projected at 3.3 percent both in 2025 and 2026, below the historical (2000–19) average of 3.7 percent. The forecast is broadly unchanged from the October 2024 WEO, primarily on account of an upward revision in the United States offsetting downward revisions in other major economies. Global headline inflation is expected to decline to 4.2 percent in 2025 and 3.5 percent in 2026, converging back to target earlier in advanced economies than in emerging market and developing economies. Medium-term risks to the baseline are tilted to the downside, while the near-term outlook is characterized by divergent risks. Upside risks could lift already-robust growth in the United States in the short run, whereas risks in other countries are on the downside amid elevated policy uncertainty. Policy-generated disruptions to the ongoing disinflation process could interrupt the pivot to easing monetary policy, with implications for fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Key risks: renewed inflationary pressures, trade policy uncertainty (US tariff proposals), geopolitical disruptions, abrupt shift in market sentiment. Country highlights: US growth revised up to 2.7% for 2025; euro area revised down to 1.0%; China growth 4.5%.

scenarios.title: Stronger Swiss franc squeezes exporters and monetary policy
scenarios.narration:
Divergent interest-rate moves by major central banks could draw more safe-haven money into Swiss franc assets. The Bank of Japan raised its rate in January 2025 while the European Central Bank cut rates and the Federal Reserve held steady. If that gap widens, investors may shift funds into the franc, pushing it stronger. Swiss exporters, especially pharmaceutical and chemical firms, and households holding foreign currency debt would feel the pressure first.

A stronger franc makes Swiss goods more expensive abroad and lowers the Swiss value of foreign earnings. Banks with large export or tourism lending could see borrower cash flows weaken. Insurance and asset managers holding foreign investments could face valuation losses. The Swiss National Bank might find its room to cut rates limited, since easing could encourage further franc outflows or weaken its inflation goal.

Wider disruption would need a sudden, large risk-off episode that triggers rapid franc appreciation and forces multiple borrowers to adjust at once. Containment could come from Swiss National Bank foreign-exchange intervention, steadier rate paths in other major economies, or improved global risk sentiment that reduces safe-haven demand.

evidence.title: Bank of Japan raises policy rate to 0.5%, the highest level since 2008
evidence.content: At its Monetary Policy Meeting of 23–24 January 2025 the Bank of Japan decided, by an 8–1 majority vote, to raise its guideline for the uncollateralised overnight call rate from around 0.25% to around 0.5%, effective 27 January 2025; board member Toyoaki Nakamura dissented. It is the first hike since July 2024 and takes the policy rate to its highest level since 2008. In its quarterly Outlook Report the Board raised the median forecast for core CPI (all items less fresh food) to 2.7% for fiscal 2024, 2.4% for fiscal 2025 (from 1.9%) and 2.0% for fiscal 2026, citing higher import prices due to the weak yen and rising rice prices, while keeping real GDP growth forecasts at 1.1% and 1.0%. The Bank expects wages and prices to keep rising in a 'virtuous cycle', noted that global financial markets have been broadly stable, and stated that it will continue to raise the policy rate if the outlook is realised. Japan's December CPI, released the same day, rose 3.6% year on year. The yen strengthened by about 0.5% to around 155 per US dollar after the decision; higher Japanese rates are watched as a risk to yen-funded carry trades and as a factor for safe-haven flows into the Swiss franc.

evidence.content: On 30 January 2025, the ECB Governing Council decided to lower the three key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. evidence.title: Fed FOMC January 2025 – Rates Held at 4.25-4.50% (Hawkish Hold)
evidence.content: The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady at 4.25-4.50% at the January 28-29, 2025 FOMC meeting. This marks a pause in the rate-cutting cycle after 100 basis points of cuts in 2024 (Sep, Nov, Dec). Chair Powell stated the Fed is 'not in a hurry' to adjust policy. Solid labor market, inflation remains 'somewhat elevated'. Decision: unanimous 12-0.

evidence.title: Swiss consumer prices fell 0.1% in December 2024; average annual inflation of 1.1% in 2024
evidence.content: The Swiss Federal Statistical Office (FSO) reported on 7 January 2025 that the national consumer price index fell by 0.1% in December 2024 compared with the previous month, to 106.9 points (December 2020 = 100). Inflation was +0.6% compared with December 2023, after +0.7% in November. The decline in December was due to lower prices for package holidays abroad, medicines and various vegetables, while prices for hotel and supplementary accommodation rose. Food and non-alcoholic beverages were 0.9% cheaper and transport 1.9% cheaper than a year earlier. Average annual inflation reached +1.1% in 2024, after 2.1% in 2023 and 2.8% in 2022, with a high of 1.4% (April, May) and a low of 0.6% (October, December), well within the Swiss National Bank's definition of price stability (0–2%). Household electricity tariffs were cut by around 10% on average at the start of 2025, and the SNB's conditional forecast of December 2024 expects inflation of 0.3% for 2025.

evidence.title: BIS Innovation Hub sets out 2025–26 work programme: AI-enabled supervision and green finance
evidence.content: On 14 January 2025 the Bank for International Settlements published the 2025–26 work programme of its Innovation Hub. At the start of 2025 the Hub's portfolio comprised 26 active projects, with 31 projects completed since its establishment in 2019 and 16 new projects started in 2024. The first two new projects of 2025 will develop AI-enabled tools, one to support financial regulation and supervision (suptech) and one for green finance. The Hub's ongoing work on tokenisation and next-generation financial market infrastructure includes the Project Agorá initiative with seven central banks and more than 40 private financial firms exploring tokenised correspondent banking for cross-border payments, and aims to exploit synergies across the existing project portfolio. The Hub serves as a focal point for a network of central bank innovation experts; its Swiss Centre is hosted in Zurich in cooperation with the Swiss National Bank.

evidence.title: FSB Work Programme for 2025
evidence.content: The FSB published its Work Programme for 2025 on 23 January 2025, outlining key regulatory and financial stability priorities for the year. Priority areas: (1) Supporting global cooperation on financial stability; (2) Enhancing resilience of non-bank financial intermediation (NBFI) while preserving its benefits – major G20 deliverable; (3) Harnessing benefits of digital innovation (crypto-assets, AI in finance, cross-border payments) while containing risks – major G20 deliverable; (4) Implementing the systemically important financial institution (SIFI) framework; (5) Addressing financial risks from climate change – climate roadmap progress; (6) Enhancing cross-border payments; (7) Completing resolution reforms. Key G20 deliverables planned: NBFI leverage policy recommendations (Jul 2025); Vulnerabilities from AI in finance (Oct 2025); Thematic peer review on crypto-assets (Oct 2025); FSB Annual Report (Dec 2025). Context: FSB is chaired by Klaas Knot (DNB). Secretariat in Basel, hosted by BIS.

evidence.title: FSB: Analytical Framework and Toolkit to Assess Climate-Related Vulnerabilities
evidence.content: The FSB published on 16 January 2025 a new analytical framework and toolkit to assess climate-related vulnerabilities in the global financial system. Key elements: (1) Framework traces how physical and transition climate risks transmit and amplify within the global financial system, building on the FSB Financial Stability Surveillance Framework. (2) Three categories of forward-looking toolkit metrics: proxies (early signals on drivers of transition/physical risks); exposure metrics (direct and indirect exposures in real economy and financial system); risk metrics (quantify impacts for financial institutions). (3) Case study: crystallisation of physical climate risks via real estate markets and changes in insurance coverage. Quotes: 'The framework provides a forward-looking approach to capture the unique aspects of climate risks while staying rooted in traditional financial stability analysis' (Sarah Breeden, Bank of England Deputy Governor). Policy area: Climate-related Risks. Ref: 2/2025. Part of FSB Roadmap to Address Climate-related Financial Risks (G20 mandate, July 2021).

evidence.title: Confirmed: 2024 was the hottest year on record, says UN weather agency
evidence.content: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) confirmed on 10 January 2025 that 2024 was the warmest year on record, based on six international datasets. The global average surface temperature was 1.55 °C (±0.13 °C) above the 1850–1900 average, which means the world has likely experienced the first calendar year more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels. The past ten years, 2015–2024, are the ten warmest on record, and ocean heat content reached a new record. 'Climate history is playing out before our eyes', said WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo, citing devastating extreme weather, rising sea levels and melting ice. WMO stressed that a single year above 1.5 °C does not mean that the long-term Paris Agreement goal, measured over decades, has been missed, but that every fraction of a degree of warming increases impacts on lives, economies and the planet. UN Secretary-General António Guterres called on governments to deliver new national climate action plans in 2025.

evidence.title: Munich Re: natural disasters caused USD 140 billion of insured losses in 2024 as Los Angeles wildfires start 2025
evidence.content: According to the reinsurer Munich Re's annual natural catastrophe report of 9 January 2025, natural disasters caused overall losses of USD 320 billion in 2024 (2023: USD 268 billion), of which USD 140 billion were insured – the third-highest insured total since 1980, the highest since 2017 and almost 50% above the ten-year average. Weather-related events accounted for 93% of overall and 97% of insured losses; hurricanes Helene and Milton in the United States were the costliest events, and 'non-peak' perils such as floods, wildfires and severe thunderstorms caused USD 136 billion of losses, about USD 67 billion of them insured. About 11,000 people died in natural disasters. 'Climate change is showing its claws', Munich Re said. The report was published as wildfires were destroying large parts of Los Angeles, threatening to become the costliest wildfire on record; California prohibited insurers from cancelling or not renewing home policies in the affected areas. With mounting claims, the cost of reinsurance is rising.

evidence.title: SNB data portal: EUR/CHF monthly average of 0.9416 in January 2025
evidence.content: According to the Swiss National Bank's data portal (cube 'devkum', monthly averages of foreign exchange rates, 11:00 fixing), the euro traded at an average of 0.94162 Swiss francs in January 2025. The franc thus remained close to its strongest levels against the euro, after the SNB had cut its policy rate by 50 basis points to 0.5% in December 2024 and stated that it remains willing to intervene in the foreign exchange market as necessary. The EUR/CHF rate is a key transmission channel for imported inflation in Switzerland and a central reference variable for the SNB's monetary policy.

evidence.title: Swiss foreign trade 2024: record exports driven almost entirely by chemicals and pharmaceuticals
evidence.content: The Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS/BAZG) reported on 30 January 2025 that Swiss exports rose by 3.2% (real: +2.5%) to a record CHF 282.9 billion in 2024, after declines in both directions of trade in 2023. The record was achieved almost exclusively by the chemical-pharmaceutical sector, whose exports grew by 10.0% (medicines +7.7%) and which accounts for more than half of total exports; exports of chemical-pharmaceutical raw and basic materials doubled within a year. Most other product groups recorded falling foreign sales: watch exports declined by 2.8% and jewellery by 4.5% after record years. Imports fell by 1.6% to CHF 222.3 billion, with imports from Asia at their lowest level since 2020. The opposing trends resulted in a record trade surplus of CHF 60.6 billion. The concentration on a single sector makes Swiss exports sensitive to sector-specific trade policy measures such as tariffs on pharmaceuticals.

evidence.content: IMF World Economic Outlook Update, January 2025: 'Global Growth: Divergent and Uncertain'. Published January 17, 2025. The forecast is broadly unchanged from the October 2024 WEO, primarily on account of an upward revision in the United States offsetting downward revisions in other major economies. evidence.title: UK 30-year gilt yields rise to highest level since 1998 amid concerns over public finances
evidence.content: UK long-term borrowing costs rose to their highest level in more than a quarter of a century in early January 2025. On 7 January the Debt Management Office auctioned GBP 2.25 billion of 30-year gilts at a yield of 5.198%, and the 30-year yield climbed to 5.37% on 8 January, the highest since 1998 and above the levels of the 2022 'mini-budget' crisis; the 10-year yield rose to around 4.8–4.9%, the highest since 2008. Sterling fell to about USD 1.22, its lowest since November 2023. The sell-off was part of a global rise in long-dated government bond yields led by US Treasuries, but was amplified by near-record UK debt issuance of about GBP 297 billion in the 2024–25 fiscal year, persistent inflation and economic stagnation. Analysts warned that higher interest costs could erase the GBP 9.9 billion of fiscal headroom left by the October budget, forcing Chancellor Rachel Reeves to cut spending or raise taxes again; the Treasury said the fiscal rules are 'non-negotiable'.

evidence.title: Swiss Federal Council opens consultation on 'relief package 27' to stabilise federal finances
evidence.content: At its meeting on 29 January 2025 the Swiss Federal Council adopted the consultation draft of relief package 27 (RP27) and opened the consultation, which runs until 5 May 2025. The package of 59 measures is intended to reduce the federal budget by about CHF 2.7 billion in 2027 and CHF 3.6 billion in 2028, so that the debt brake can be respected despite rising expenditure for the armed forces and the old-age pension system (including the 13th AHV pension). More than half of the measures require amendments to federal law. The proposals include cuts of more than CHF 460 million per year in education, research and innovation, as well as higher taxation of capital withdrawals from the second and third pillars. Even with the package, federal expenditure is expected to grow by more than 2% per year in the medium term. Several parties and the cantons had already criticised the proposals in autumn 2024, so the package is expected to be politically contested.

scenarios.title: Tech equity sell-off shrinks Swiss central bank profit
scenarios.narration:
A sharp fall in global technology equities could cut the market value of shares held in central bank reserves. The Swiss National Bank earned a record profit in 2024, but its result depends heavily on exchange rates and financial market developments and is very volatile. A sudden equity sell-off would create mark-to-market losses on those holdings.

Smaller investment income would shrink the profit the SNB can distribute to the Confederation and cantons. If payouts fall, public budgets lose revenue. That could pressure cantons to cut spending or raise taxes, touching households and businesses. The SNB might also hold back earnings to rebuild currency-reserve provisions, further reducing distributions.

Wider disruption would require losses big enough to strain the SNB's capital or force large asset sales that move markets. Current equity volatility is close to its long-term median, so that outcome is not signaled now. Capital buffers, retained earnings, and the SNB's ability to supply Swiss-franc liquidity could contain the effect.

evidence.title: DeepSeek shock: Nvidia loses about USD 590 billion in market value in record one-day drop
evidence.content: On 27 January 2025 global technology stocks sold off after the Chinese start-up DeepSeek showed that its AI models can match leading US models at a fraction of the cost. Nvidia shares fell almost 17%, erasing about USD 589 billion of market capitalisation, the largest one-day loss of market value for any company in US stock market history and more than double Nvidia's previous record from September 2024. Broadcom fell 17%, TSMC 13%, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 3.1% while the S&P 500 fell 1.5%. DeepSeek-V3, launched on 10 January, was reportedly trained on Nvidia's lower-capability H800 chips for less than USD 6 million, and DeepSeek-R1, released the previous week, is reportedly 20 to 50 times cheaper to use than OpenAI's comparable model. Before the sell-off Nvidia traded at nearly 60 times earnings, compared with 22 for the S&P 500; the sell-off raised questions about the valuations and the very large AI investment plans of US technology firms.

evidence.title: Swiss consumer prices fell 0.1% in December 2024; average annual inflation of 1.1% in 2024
evidence.content: The Swiss Federal Statistical Office (FSO) reported on 7 January 2025 that the national consumer price index fell by 0.1% in December 2024 compared with the previous month, to 106.9 points (December 2020 = 100). Inflation was +0.6% compared with December 2023, after +0.7% in November. The decline in December was due to lower prices for package holidays abroad, medicines and various vegetables, while prices for hotel and supplementary accommodation rose. Food and non-alcoholic beverages were 0.9% cheaper and transport 1.9% cheaper than a year earlier. Average annual inflation reached +1.1% in 2024, after 2.1% in 2023 and 2.8% in 2022, with a high of 1.4% (April, May) and a low of 0.6% (October, December), well within the Swiss National Bank's definition of price stability (0–2%). evidence.title: BIS Innovation Hub sets out 2025–26 work programme: AI-enabled supervision and green finance
evidence.content: On 14 January 2025 the Bank for International Settlements published the 2025–26 work programme of its Innovation Hub. The first two new projects of 2025 will develop AI-enabled tools, one to support financial regulation and supervision (suptech) and one for green finance. evidence.title: FSB Work Programme for 2025
evidence.content: The FSB published its Work Programme for 2025 on 23 January 2025, outlining key regulatory and financial stability priorities for the year. Priority areas: (1) Supporting global cooperation on financial stability; (2) Enhancing resilience of non-bank financial intermediation (NBFI) while preserving its benefits – major G20 deliverable; (3) Harnessing benefits of digital innovation (crypto-assets, AI in finance, cross-border payments) while containing risks – major G20 deliverable; (4) Implementing the systemically important financial institution (SIFI) framework; (5) Addressing financial risks from climate change – climate roadmap progress; (6) Enhancing cross-border payments; (7) Completing resolution reforms. evidence.title: FSB: Analytical Framework and Toolkit to Assess Climate-Related Vulnerabilities
evidence.content: The FSB published on 16 January 2025 a new analytical framework and toolkit to assess climate-related vulnerabilities in the global financial system. Key elements: (1) Framework traces how physical and transition climate risks transmit and amplify within the global financial system, building on the FSB Financial Stability Surveillance Framework. (2) Three categories of forward-looking toolkit metrics: proxies (early signals on drivers of transition/physical risks); exposure metrics (direct and indirect exposures in real economy and financial system); risk metrics (quantify impacts for financial institutions). (3) Case study: crystallisation of physical climate risks via real estate markets and changes in insurance coverage. evidence.title: Confirmed: 2024 was the hottest year on record, says UN weather agency
evidence.content: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) confirmed on 10 January 2025 that 2024 was the warmest year on record, based on six international datasets. The global average surface temperature was 1.55 °C (±0.13 °C) above the 1850–1900 average, which means the world has likely experienced the first calendar year more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels. The past ten years, 2015–2024, are the ten warmest on record, and ocean heat content reached a new record. 'Climate history is playing out before our eyes', said WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo, citing devastating extreme weather, rising sea levels and melting ice. WMO stressed that a single year above 1.5 °C does not mean that the long-term Paris Agreement goal, measured over decades, has been missed, but that every fraction of a degree of warming increases impacts on lives, economies and the planet. UN Secretary-General António Guterres called on governments to deliver new national climate action plans in 2025.

evidence.title: Munich Re: natural disasters caused USD 140 billion of insured losses in 2024 as Los Angeles wildfires start 2025
evidence.content: According to the reinsurer Munich Re's annual natural catastrophe report of 9 January 2025, natural disasters caused overall losses of USD 320 billion in 2024 (2023: USD 268 billion), of which USD 140 billion were insured – the third-highest insured total since 1980, the highest since 2017 and almost 50% above the ten-year average. Weather-related events accounted for 93% of overall and 97% of insured losses; hurricanes Helene and Milton in the United States were the costliest events, and 'non-peak' perils such as floods, wildfires and severe thunderstorms caused USD 136 billion of losses, about USD 67 billion of them insured. About 11,000 people died in natural disasters. 'Climate change is showing its claws', Munich Re said. The report was published as wildfires were destroying large parts of Los Angeles, threatening to become the costliest wildfire on record; California prohibited insurers from cancelling or not renewing home policies in the affected areas. With mounting claims, the cost of reinsurance is rising.

evidence.title: SNB expects record annual profit of around CHF 80 billion for 2024, resumes distribution to Confederation and cantons
evidence.content: According to provisional calculations published on 9 January 2025, the Swiss National Bank will report a profit of around CHF 80 billion for 2024, after a loss of CHF 3.2 billion in 2023 and well above the previous record of CHF 54.4 billion in 2017. The result consists of a profit of around CHF 67 billion on foreign currency positions, a valuation gain of CHF 21.2 billion on gold holdings and a loss of CHF 7.4 billion on Swiss franc positions; the foreign currency result benefited from rising equity markets, a stronger US dollar and a higher gold price. After an allocation of CHF 11.6 billion to the provisions for currency reserves and taking into account the negative distribution reserve of CHF 53.2 billion, the net profit amounts to about CHF 16 billion. This allows the legal maximum dividend of CHF 15 per share and a distribution of CHF 3 billion to the Confederation (one third) and the cantons (two thirds), after two years without a distribution. The SNB's result depends heavily on exchange rates and financial market developments and is therefore very volatile.

evidence.title: Swiss foreign trade 2024: record exports driven almost entirely by chemicals and pharmaceuticals
evidence.content: The Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS/BAZG) reported on 30 January 2025 that Swiss exports rose by 3.2% (real: +2.5%) to a record CHF 282.9 billion in 2024, after declines in both directions of trade in 2023. The record was achieved almost exclusively by the chemical-pharmaceutical sector, whose exports grew by 10.0% (medicines +7.7%) and which accounts for more than half of total exports; exports of chemical-pharmaceutical raw and basic materials doubled within a year. Most other product groups recorded falling foreign sales: watch exports declined by 2.8% and jewellery by 4.5% after record years. Imports fell by 1.6% to CHF 222.3 billion, with imports from Asia at their lowest level since 2020. The opposing trends resulted in a record trade surplus of CHF 60.6 billion. The concentration on a single sector makes Swiss exports sensitive to sector-specific trade policy measures such as tariffs on pharmaceuticals.

evidence.title: UK 30-year gilt yields rise to highest level since 1998 amid concerns over public finances
evidence.content: UK long-term borrowing costs rose to their highest level in more than a quarter of a century in early January 2025. On 7 January the Debt Management Office auctioned GBP 2.25 billion of 30-year gilts at a yield of 5.198%, and the 30-year yield climbed to 5.37% on 8 January, the highest since 1998 and above the levels of the 2022 'mini-budget' crisis; the 10-year yield rose to around 4.8–4.9%, the highest since 2008. Sterling fell to about USD 1.22, its lowest since November 2023. The sell-off was part of a global rise in long-dated government bond yields led by US Treasuries, but was amplified by near-record UK debt issuance of about GBP 297 billion in the 2024–25 fiscal year, persistent inflation and economic stagnation. Analysts warned that higher interest costs could erase the GBP 9.9 billion of fiscal headroom left by the October budget, forcing Chancellor Rachel Reeves to cut spending or raise taxes again; the Treasury said the fiscal rules are 'non-negotiable'.

evidence.title: Swiss Federal Council opens consultation on 'relief package 27' to stabilise federal finances
evidence.content: At its meeting on 29 January 2025 the Swiss Federal Council adopted the consultation draft of relief package 27 (RP27) and opened the consultation, which runs until 5 May 2025. The package of 59 measures is intended to reduce the federal budget by about CHF 2.7 billion in 2027 and CHF 3.6 billion in 2028, so that the debt brake can be respected despite rising expenditure for the armed forces and the old-age pension system (including the 13th AHV pension). More than half of the measures require amendments to federal law. The proposals include cuts of more than CHF 460 million per year in education, research and innovation, as well as higher taxation of capital withdrawals from the second and third pillars. Even with the package, federal expenditure is expected to grow by more than 2% per year in the medium term. Several parties and the cantons had already criticised the proposals in autumn 2024, so the package is expected to be politically contested.

scenarios.title: Tokenised dollar settlement freeze disrupts cross-border payments
scenarios.narration:
More cross-border payments are moving onto tokenised platforms run by a small group of private issuers. If geopolitical tensions disrupt existing payment corridors, businesses and investors could rush to exit these tokenised balances at once. Households and firms that rely on dollar settlement for trade and invoicing would be directly affected.

A sudden redemption rush could freeze transfers through the issuer's network. Banks that hold these tokens as settlement assets could find them hard to sell or use as collateral. Payment delays could ripple to suppliers, exporters and importers, forcing businesses to delay wages or shipments and households to miss bill payments.

Wider disruption would need several large issuers to fail at once or a loss of confidence in tokenised dollars generally. Central bank liquidity facilities and existing payment rails could contain the impact if they remain accessible and trusted. Regulators would need to check whether issuers hold enough liquid reserves to meet outflows.

evidence.title: US Executive Order 14178 'Strengthening American Leadership in Digital Financial Technology' prohibits a US CBDC
evidence.content: On 23 January 2025 the US President signed Executive Order 14178, setting the policy of the new administration to 'support the responsible growth and use of digital assets, blockchain technology, and related technologies across all sectors of the economy'. The order prohibits agencies from establishing, issuing, circulating or promoting a central bank digital currency (CBDC) within the United States and halts ongoing CBDC initiatives. It promotes the development of lawful and legitimate dollar-backed stablecoins worldwide to protect the sovereignty of the US dollar, calls for regulatory clarity based on well-defined jurisdictional boundaries, and protects access to banking services for digital-asset firms. A President's Working Group on Digital Asset Markets is established to propose a federal regulatory framework for digital assets, including stablecoins, and to evaluate a possible national digital asset stockpile. The order revokes Executive Order 14067 of 2022 and the Treasury's 'Framework for International Engagement on Digital Assets'. On the same day the SEC rescinded its Staff Accounting Bulletin 121 on crypto-asset custody.

Household electricity tariffs were cut by around 10% on average at the start of 2025, and the SNB's conditional forecast of December 2024 expects inflation of 0.3% for 2025.

evidence.title: FSB Work Programme for 2025
evidence.content: The FSB published its Work Programme for 2025 on 23 January 2025, outlining key regulatory and financial stability priorities for the year. Priority areas: (1) Supporting global cooperation on financial stability; (2) Enhancing resilience of non-bank financial intermediation (NBFI) while preserving its benefits – major G20 deliverable; (3) Harnessing benefits of digital innovation (crypto-assets, AI in finance, cross-border payments) while containing risks – major G20 deliverable; (4) Implementing the systemically important financial institution (SIFI) framework; (5) Addressing financial risks from climate change – climate roadmap progress; (6) Enhancing cross-border payments; (7) Completing resolution reforms. Key G20 deliverables planned: NBFI leverage policy recommendations (Jul 2025); Vulnerabilities from AI in finance (Oct 2025); Thematic peer review on crypto-assets (Oct 2025); FSB Annual Report (Dec 2025). Context: FSB is chaired by Klaas Knot (DNB). Secretariat in Basel, hosted by BIS.

evidence.title: FSB: Analytical Framework and Toolkit to Assess Climate-Related Vulnerabilities
evidence.content: The FSB published on 16 January 2025 a new analytical framework and toolkit to assess climate-related vulnerabilities in the global financial system. Key elements: (1) Framework traces how physical and transition climate risks transmit and amplify within the global financial system, building on the FSB Financial Stability Surveillance Framework. (2) Three categories of forward-looking toolkit metrics: proxies (early signals on drivers of transition/physical risks); exposure metrics (direct and indirect exposures in real economy and financial system); risk metrics (quantify impacts for financial institutions). (3) Case study: crystallisation of physical climate risks via real estate markets and changes in insurance coverage. Quotes: 'The framework provides a forward-looking approach to capture the unique aspects of climate risks while staying rooted in traditional financial stability analysis' (Sarah Breeden, Bank of England Deputy Governor). Policy area: Climate-related Risks. Ref: 2/2025. Part of FSB Roadmap to Address Climate-related Financial Risks (G20 mandate, July 2021).

evidence.title: Confirmed: 2024 was the hottest year on record, says UN weather agency
evidence.content: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) confirmed on 10 January 2025 that 2024 was the warmest year on record, based on six international datasets. The global average surface temperature was 1.55 °C (±0.13 °C) above the 1850–1900 average, which means the world has likely experienced the first calendar year more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels. The past ten years, 2015–2024, are the ten warmest on record, and ocean heat content reached a new record. 'Climate history is playing out before our eyes', said WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo, citing devastating extreme weather, rising sea levels and melting ice. WMO stressed that a single year above 1.5 °C does not mean that the long-term Paris Agreement goal, measured over decades, has been missed, but that every fraction of a degree of warming increases impacts on lives, economies and the planet. UN Secretary-General António Guterres called on governments to deliver new national climate action plans in 2025.

evidence.title: Munich Re: natural disasters caused USD 140 billion of insured losses in 2024 as Los Angeles wildfires start 2025
evidence.content: According to the reinsurer Munich Re's annual natural catastrophe report of 9 January 2025, natural disasters caused overall losses of USD 320 billion in 2024 (2023: USD 268 billion), of which USD 140 billion were insured – the third-highest insured total since 1980, the highest since 2017 and almost 50% above the ten-year average. Weather-related events accounted for 93% of overall and 97% of insured losses; hurricanes Helene and Milton in the United States were the costliest events, and 'non-peak' perils such as floods, wildfires and severe thunderstorms caused USD 136 billion of losses, about USD 67 billion of them insured. About 11,000 people died in natural disasters. 'Climate change is showing its claws', Munich Re said. The report was published as wildfires were destroying large parts of Los Angeles, threatening to become the costliest wildfire on record; California prohibited insurers from cancelling or not renewing home policies in the affected areas. With mounting claims, the cost of reinsurance is rising.

evidence.title: SNB data portal: EUR/CHF monthly average of 0.9416 in January 2025
evidence.content: According to the Swiss National Bank's data portal (cube 'devkum', monthly averages of foreign exchange rates, 11:00 fixing), the euro traded at an average of 0.94162 Swiss francs in January 2025. The franc thus remained close to its strongest levels against the euro, after the SNB had cut its policy rate by 50 basis points to 0.5% in December 2024 and stated that it remains willing to intervene in the foreign exchange market as necessary. The EUR/CHF rate is a key transmission channel for imported inflation in Switzerland and a central reference variable for the SNB's monetary policy.

evidence.title: Swiss foreign trade 2024: record exports driven almost entirely by chemicals and pharmaceuticals
evidence.content: The Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS/BAZG) reported on 30 January 2025 that Swiss exports rose by 3.2% (real: +2.5%) to a record CHF 282.9 billion in 2024, after declines in both directions of trade in 2023. The record was achieved almost exclusively by the chemical-pharmaceutical sector, whose exports grew by 10.0% (medicines +7.7%) and which accounts for more than half of total exports; exports of chemical-pharmaceutical raw and basic materials doubled within a year. Most other product groups recorded falling foreign sales: watch exports declined by 2.8% and jewellery by 4.5% after record years. Imports fell by 1.6% to CHF 222.3 billion, with imports from Asia at their lowest level since 2020. The opposing trends resulted in a record trade surplus of CHF 60.6 billion. The concentration on a single sector makes Swiss exports sensitive to sector-specific trade policy measures such as tariffs on pharmaceuticals.

evidence.title: EU Council extends economic sanctions against Russia for six months, until 31 July 2025
evidence.content: On 27 January 2025 the Council of the European Union renewed its economic restrictive measures against Russia for a further six months, until 31 July 2025. The sanctions, first introduced in 2014 and significantly expanded since February 2022, cover trade, finance, energy, technology, dual-use goods, industry, transport and luxury goods, including the ban on imports of seaborne crude oil and certain petroleum products, the exclusion of Russian banks from SWIFT and the immobilisation of Russian central bank assets of around EUR 210 billion. Renewal requires unanimity: Hungary had threatened for weeks to block the extension and lifted its objection after receiving a declaration on its energy security following the end of gas transit through Ukraine. Since February 2022 the EU has adopted 15 sanctions packages; a 16th package is being prepared for the third anniversary of the invasion on 24 February 2025. Switzerland, which aligns with EU sanctions, had added 54 individuals and 30 entities to its Russia list on 23 December 2024.

evidence.title: OFAC sanctions Chinese firm linked to Salt Typhoon telecom hacks and hacker involved in US Treasury breach
evidence.content: On 17 January 2025 the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned Yin Kecheng, a Shanghai-based cyber actor affiliated with China's Ministry of State Security, for his involvement in the recent compromise of the Treasury Department's Departmental Offices network, which Treasury had detected on 8 December 2024. OFAC also designated Sichuan Juxinhe Network Technology, a cybersecurity company with direct involvement in the Salt Typhoon group, which recently compromised the network infrastructure of multiple major US telecommunication and internet service providers, including AT&T and Verizon, to access private communications. Treasury described the intrusions as an example of an increasing number of PRC state-backed cyber activities that require costly remediation; the action follows the designation of Integrity Technology Group on 3 January for its role in the Flax Typhoon intrusions. All property of the designated persons in the United States is blocked.

evidence.title: IMF WEO Update January 2025 – Global Growth 3.3%, US Upgraded, Trade Policy Risk
evidence.content: IMF World Economic Outlook Update, January 2025: 'Global Growth: Divergent and Uncertain'. Published January 17, 2025. Global growth is projected at 3.3 percent both in 2025 and 2026, below the historical (2000–19) average of 3.7 percent. The forecast is broadly unchanged from the October 2024 WEO, primarily on account of an upward revision in the United States offsetting downward revisions in other major economies. Global headline inflation is expected to decline to 4.2 percent in 2025 and 3.5 percent in 2026, converging back to target earlier in advanced economies than in emerging market and developing economies. proto_modules.name: Global Financial Spillover Channels
proto_modules.novelty_rationale: The shift from ultra-low Japanese interest rates to policy normalization is a regime change after decades, reactivating carry trade unwinding as a structural transmission channel, while cross-border spillover mechanisms themselves are longstanding.
proto_modules.reasoning: The implications describe distinct but linked channels through which global macroeconomic and monetary divergences transmit across borders to financial stability: leveraged carry trade positions unwind as rate differentials narrow, uneven growth spreads through trade and banking exposures, and elevated uncertainty tightens financial conditions via risk premia and sentiment. Together they form a subsystem of cross-border financial spillovers where external shocks propagate through capital flows, banking linkages, and market sentiment.

evidence_signals.title: Bank of Japan raises policy rate to 0.5%, the highest level since 2008
evidence_signals.content: At its Monetary Policy Meeting of 23–24 January 2025 the Bank of Japan decided, by an 8–1 majority vote, to raise its guideline for the uncollateralised overnight call rate from around 0.25% to around 0.5%, effective 27 January 2025; board member Toyoaki Nakamura dissented. It is the first hike since July 2024 and takes the policy rate to its highest level since 2008. In its quarterly Outlook Report the Board raised the median forecast for core CPI (all items less fresh food) to 2.7% for fiscal 2024, 2.4% for fiscal 2025 (from 1.9%) and 2.0% for fiscal 2026, citing higher import prices due to the weak yen and rising rice prices, while keeping real GDP growth forecasts at 1.1% and 1.0%. The Bank expects wages and prices to keep rising in a 'virtuous cycle', noted that global financial markets have been broadly stable, and stated that it will continue to raise the policy rate if the outlook is realised. Japan's December CPI, released the same day, rose 3.6% year on year. The yen strengthened by about 0.5% to around 155 per US dollar after the decision; higher Japanese rates are watched as a risk to yen-funded carry trades and as a factor for safe-haven flows into the Swiss franc.

scenario.title: Stronger Swiss franc squeezes exporters and monetary policy
scenario.narration:
Divergent interest-rate moves by major central banks could draw more safe-haven money into Swiss franc assets. The Bank of Japan raised its rate in January 2025 while the European Central Bank cut rates and the Federal Reserve held steady. If that gap widens, investors may shift funds into the franc, pushing it stronger. Swiss exporters, especially pharmaceutical and chemical firms, and households holding foreign currency debt would feel the pressure first.

A stronger franc makes Swiss goods more expensive abroad and lowers the Swiss value of foreign earnings. Banks with large export or tourism lending could see borrower cash flows weaken. Insurance and asset managers holding foreign investments could face valuation losses. The Swiss National Bank might find its room to cut rates limited, since easing could encourage further franc outflows or weaken its inflation goal.

Wider disruption would need a sudden, large risk-off episode that triggers rapid franc appreciation and forces multiple borrowers to adjust at once. Containment could come from Swiss National Bank foreign-exchange intervention, steadier rate paths in other major economies, or improved global risk sentiment that reduces safe-haven demand.

evidence.title: Bank of Japan raises policy rate to 0.5%, the highest level since 2008
evidence.content: At its Monetary Policy Meeting of 23–24 January 2025 the Bank of Japan decided, by an 8–1 majority vote, to raise its guideline for the uncollateralised overnight call rate from around 0.25% to around 0.5%, effective 27 January 2025; board member Toyoaki Nakamura dissented. It is the first hike since July 2024 and takes the policy rate to its highest level since 2008. In its quarterly Outlook Report the Board raised the median forecast for core CPI (all items less fresh food) to 2.7% for fiscal 2024, 2.4% for fiscal 2025 (from 1.9%) and 2.0% for fiscal 2026, citing higher import prices due to the weak yen and rising rice prices, while keeping real GDP growth forecasts at 1.1% and 1.0%. The Bank expects wages and prices to keep rising in a 'virtuous cycle', noted that global financial markets have been broadly stable, and stated that it will continue to raise the policy rate if the outlook is realised. Japan's December CPI, released the same day, rose 3.6% year on year. The yen strengthened by about 0.5% to around 155 per US dollar after the decision; higher Japanese rates are watched as a risk to yen-funded carry trades and as a factor for safe-haven flows into the Swiss franc.

evidence.content: The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady at 4.25-4.50% at the January 28-29, 2025 FOMC meeting.
