evidence.title: Swiss consumer prices fell 0.1% in December 2024; average annual inflation of 1.1% in 2024
evidence.content: The Swiss Federal Statistical Office (FSO) reported on 7 January 2025 that the national consumer price index fell by 0.1% in December 2024 compared with the previous month, to 106.9 points (December 2020 = 100). Inflation was +0.6% compared with December 2023, after +0.7% in November. The decline in December was due to lower prices for package holidays abroad, medicines and various vegetables, while prices for hotel and supplementary accommodation rose. Food and non-alcoholic beverages were 0.9% cheaper and transport 1.9% cheaper than a year earlier. Average annual inflation reached +1.1% in 2024, after 2.1% in 2023 and 2.8% in 2022, with a high of 1.4% (April, May) and a low of 0.6% (October, December), well within the Swiss National Bank's definition of price stability (0–2%). Household electricity tariffs were cut by around 10% on average at the start of 2025, and the SNB's conditional forecast of December 2024 expects inflation of 0.3% for 2025.

evidence.title: BIS Innovation Hub sets out 2025–26 work programme: AI-enabled supervision and green finance
evidence.content: On 14 January 2025 the Bank for International Settlements published the 2025–26 work programme of its Innovation Hub. At the start of 2025 the Hub's portfolio comprised 26 active projects, with 31 projects completed since its establishment in 2019 and 16 new projects started in 2024. The first two new projects of 2025 will develop AI-enabled tools, one to support financial regulation and supervision (suptech) and one for green finance. The Hub's ongoing work on tokenisation and next-generation financial market infrastructure includes the Project Agorá initiative with seven central banks and more than 40 private financial firms exploring tokenised correspondent banking for cross-border payments, and aims to exploit synergies across the existing project portfolio. The Hub serves as a focal point for a network of central bank innovation experts; its Swiss Centre is hosted in Zurich in cooperation with the Swiss National Bank.

evidence.title: FSB Work Programme for 2025
evidence.content: The FSB published its Work Programme for 2025 on 23 January 2025, outlining key regulatory and financial stability priorities for the year. Priority areas: (1) Supporting global cooperation on financial stability; (2) Enhancing resilience of non-bank financial intermediation (NBFI) while preserving its benefits – major G20 deliverable; (3) Harnessing benefits of digital innovation (crypto-assets, AI in finance, cross-border payments) while containing risks – major G20 deliverable; (4) Implementing the systemically important financial institution (SIFI) framework; (5) Addressing financial risks from climate change – climate roadmap progress; (6) Enhancing cross-border payments; (7) Completing resolution reforms. Key G20 deliverables planned: NBFI leverage policy recommendations (Jul 2025); Vulnerabilities from AI in finance (Oct 2025); Thematic peer review on crypto-assets (Oct 2025); FSB Annual Report (Dec 2025). Context: FSB is chaired by Klaas Knot (DNB). Secretariat in Basel, hosted by BIS.

evidence.title: FSB: Analytical Framework and Toolkit to Assess Climate-Related Vulnerabilities
evidence.content: The FSB published on 16 January 2025 a new analytical framework and toolkit to assess climate-related vulnerabilities in the global financial system. Key elements: (1) Framework traces how physical and transition climate risks transmit and amplify within the global financial system, building on the FSB Financial Stability Surveillance Framework. (2) Three categories of forward-looking toolkit metrics: proxies (early signals on drivers of transition/physical risks); exposure metrics (direct and indirect exposures in real economy and financial system); risk metrics (quantify impacts for financial institutions). (3) Case study: crystallisation of physical climate risks via real estate markets and changes in insurance coverage. Quotes: 'The framework provides a forward-looking approach to capture the unique aspects of climate risks while staying rooted in traditional financial stability analysis' (Sarah Breeden, Bank of England Deputy Governor). Policy area: Climate-related Risks. Ref: 2/2025. Part of FSB Roadmap to Address Climate-related Financial Risks (G20 mandate, July 2021).

evidence.title: Confirmed: 2024 was the hottest year on record, says UN weather agency
evidence.content: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) confirmed on 10 January 2025 that 2024 was the warmest year on record, based on six international datasets. The global average surface temperature was 1.55 °C (±0.13 °C) above the 1850–1900 average, which means the world has likely experienced the first calendar year more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels. The past ten years, 2015–2024, are the ten warmest on record, and ocean heat content reached a new record. 'Climate history is playing out before our eyes', said WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo, citing devastating extreme weather, rising sea levels and melting ice. WMO stressed that a single year above 1.5 °C does not mean that the long-term Paris Agreement goal, measured over decades, has been missed, but that every fraction of a degree of warming increases impacts on lives, economies and the planet. UN Secretary-General António Guterres called on governments to deliver new national climate action plans in 2025.

evidence.title: Munich Re: natural disasters caused USD 140 billion of insured losses in 2024 as Los Angeles wildfires start 2025
evidence.content: According to the reinsurer Munich Re's annual natural catastrophe report of 9 January 2025, natural disasters caused overall losses of USD 320 billion in 2024 (2023: USD 268 billion), of which USD 140 billion were insured – the third-highest insured total since 1980, the highest since 2017 and almost 50% above the ten-year average. Weather-related events accounted for 93% of overall and 97% of insured losses; hurricanes Helene and Milton in the United States were the costliest events, and 'non-peak' perils such as floods, wildfires and severe thunderstorms caused USD 136 billion of losses, about USD 67 billion of them insured. About 11,000 people died in natural disasters. 'Climate change is showing its claws', Munich Re said. The report was published as wildfires were destroying large parts of Los Angeles, threatening to become the costliest wildfire on record; California prohibited insurers from cancelling or not renewing home policies in the affected areas. With mounting claims, the cost of reinsurance is rising.

evidence.title: SNB data portal: EUR/CHF monthly average of 0.9416 in January 2025
evidence.content: According to the Swiss National Bank's data portal (cube 'devkum', monthly averages of foreign exchange rates, 11:00 fixing), the euro traded at an average of 0.94162 Swiss francs in January 2025. The franc thus remained close to its strongest levels against the euro, after the SNB had cut its policy rate by 50 basis points to 0.5% in December 2024 and stated that it remains willing to intervene in the foreign exchange market as necessary. The EUR/CHF rate is a key transmission channel for imported inflation in Switzerland and a central reference variable for the SNB's monetary policy.

evidence.title: Swiss foreign trade 2024: record exports driven almost entirely by chemicals and pharmaceuticals
evidence.content: The Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS/BAZG) reported on 30 January 2025 that Swiss exports rose by 3.2% (real: +2.5%) to a record CHF 282.9 billion in 2024, after declines in both directions of trade in 2023. The record was achieved almost exclusively by the chemical-pharmaceutical sector, whose exports grew by 10.0% (medicines +7.7%) and which accounts for more than half of total exports; exports of chemical-pharmaceutical raw and basic materials doubled within a year. Most other product groups recorded falling foreign sales: watch exports declined by 2.8% and jewellery by 4.5% after record years. Imports fell by 1.6% to CHF 222.3 billion, with imports from Asia at their lowest level since 2020. The opposing trends resulted in a record trade surplus of CHF 60.6 billion. The concentration on a single sector makes Swiss exports sensitive to sector-specific trade policy measures such as tariffs on pharmaceuticals.

evidence.title: UK 30-year gilt yields rise to highest level since 1998 amid concerns over public finances
evidence.content: UK long-term borrowing costs rose to their highest level in more than a quarter of a century in early January 2025. On 7 January the Debt Management Office auctioned GBP 2.25 billion of 30-year gilts at a yield of 5.198%, and the 30-year yield climbed to 5.37% on 8 January, the highest since 1998 and above the levels of the 2022 'mini-budget' crisis; the 10-year yield rose to around 4.8–4.9%, the highest since 2008. Sterling fell to about USD 1.22, its lowest since November 2023. The sell-off was part of a global rise in long-dated government bond yields led by US Treasuries, but was amplified by near-record UK debt issuance of about GBP 297 billion in the 2024–25 fiscal year, persistent inflation and economic stagnation. Analysts warned that higher interest costs could erase the GBP 9.9 billion of fiscal headroom left by the October budget, forcing Chancellor Rachel Reeves to cut spending or raise taxes again; the Treasury said the fiscal rules are 'non-negotiable'.

evidence.title: Swiss Federal Council opens consultation on 'relief package 27' to stabilise federal finances
evidence.content: At its meeting on 29 January 2025 the Swiss Federal Council adopted the consultation draft of relief package 27 (RP27) and opened the consultation, which runs until 5 May 2025. The package of 59 measures is intended to reduce the federal budget by about CHF 2.7 billion in 2027 and CHF 3.6 billion in 2028, so that the debt brake can be respected despite rising expenditure for the armed forces and the old-age pension system (including the 13th AHV pension). More than half of the measures require amendments to federal law. The proposals include cuts of more than CHF 460 million per year in education, research and innovation, as well as higher taxation of capital withdrawals from the second and third pillars. Even with the package, federal expenditure is expected to grow by more than 2% per year in the medium term. Several parties and the cantons had already criticised the proposals in autumn 2024, so the package is expected to be politically contested.

scenarios_v2.title: Trade tariffs and sanctions pressure inflation and the franc
scenarios_v2.narration:
Suppose a government uses emergency trade legislation to impose broad tariffs while, at the same time, sanctions block more banks from global payment systems. Importers, exporters and firms with cross-border contracts would face higher costs and interrupted payments. Households could see imported goods prices rise faster than incomes.

Sanctions that restrict payment networks and freeze reserves could drive investors into the Swiss franc. A stronger franc lowers Swiss import prices and makes rate cuts harder for the Swiss National Bank. Different interest-rate moves across central banks could also produce conflicting oil-demand forecasts, weakening climate risk models used by insurers and banks. Tariffs would add to sticky inflation, limiting rate cuts elsewhere.

Wider disruption would need tariffs to spread widely, sanctions to block major payment corridors, and oil forecasts to split sharply. It could be contained if central banks coordinate, alternative payment routes emerge, and oil-demand projections converge. The trade-law step remains hypothetical and might gain momentum.

evidence.title: Bank of Japan raises policy rate to 0.5%, the highest level since 2008
evidence.content: At its Monetary Policy Meeting of 23–24 January 2025 the Bank of Japan decided, by an 8–1 majority vote, to raise its guideline for the uncollateralised overnight call rate from around 0.25% to around 0.5%, effective 27 January 2025; board member Toyoaki Nakamura dissented. It is the first hike since July 2024 and takes the policy rate to its highest level since 2008. In its quarterly Outlook Report the Board raised the median forecast for core CPI (all items less fresh food) to 2.7% for fiscal 2024, 2.4% for fiscal 2025 (from 1.9%) and 2.0% for fiscal 2026, citing higher import prices due to the weak yen and rising rice prices, while keeping real GDP growth forecasts at 1.1% and 1.0%. The Bank expects wages and prices to keep rising in a 'virtuous cycle', noted that global financial markets have been broadly stable, and stated that it will continue to raise the policy rate if the outlook is realised. Japan's December CPI, released the same day, rose 3.6% year on year. The yen strengthened by about 0.5% to around 155 per US dollar after the decision; higher Japanese rates are watched as a risk to yen-funded carry trades and as a factor for safe-haven flows into the Swiss franc.

evidence.title: Swiss consumer prices fell 0.1% in December 2024; average annual inflation of 1.1% in 2024
evidence.content: The Swiss Federal Statistical Office (FSO) reported on 7 January 2025 that the national consumer price index fell by 0.1% in December 2024 compared with the previous month, to 106.9 points (December 2020 = 100). Inflation was +0.6% compared with December 2023, after +0.7% in November. The decline in December was due to lower prices for package holidays abroad, medicines and various vegetables, while prices for hotel and supplementary accommodation rose. Food and non-alcoholic beverages were 0.9% cheaper and transport 1.9% cheaper than a year earlier. Average annual inflation reached +1.1% in 2024, after 2.1% in 2023 and 2.8% in 2022, with a high of 1.4% (April, May) and a low of 0.6% (October, December), well within the Swiss National Bank's definition of price stability (0–2%). Household electricity tariffs were cut by around 10% on average at the start of 2025, and the SNB's conditional forecast of December 2024 expects inflation of 0.3% for 2025.

evidence.title: FSB: Analytical Framework and Toolkit to Assess Climate-Related Vulnerabilities
evidence.content: The FSB published on 16 January 2025 a new analytical framework and toolkit to assess climate-related vulnerabilities in the global financial system. Key elements: (1) Framework traces how physical and transition climate risks transmit and amplify within the global financial system, building on the FSB Financial Stability Surveillance Framework. (2) Three categories of forward-looking toolkit metrics: proxies (early signals on drivers of transition/physical risks); exposure metrics (direct and indirect exposures in real economy and financial system); risk metrics (quantify impacts for financial institutions). (3) Case study: crystallisation of physical climate risks via real estate markets and changes in insurance coverage. Quotes: 'The framework provides a forward-looking approach to capture the unique aspects of climate risks while staying rooted in traditional financial stability analysis' (Sarah Breeden, Bank of England Deputy Governor). Policy area: Climate-related Risks. Ref: 2/2025. Part of FSB Roadmap to Address Climate-related Financial Risks (G20 mandate, July 2021).

evidence.title: SNB data portal: EUR/CHF monthly average of 0.9416 in January 2025
evidence.content: According to the Swiss National Bank's data portal (cube 'devkum', monthly averages of foreign exchange rates, 11:00 fixing), the euro traded at an average of 0.94162 Swiss francs in January 2025. The franc thus remained close to its strongest levels against the euro, after the SNB had cut its policy rate by 50 basis points to 0.5% in December 2024 and stated that it remains willing to intervene in the foreign exchange market as necessary. The EUR/CHF rate is a key transmission channel for imported inflation in Switzerland and a central reference variable for the SNB's monetary policy.

evidence.title: EU Council extends economic sanctions against Russia for six months, until 31 July 2025
evidence.content: On 27 January 2025 the Council of the European Union renewed its economic restrictive measures against Russia for a further six months, until 31 July 2025. The sanctions, first introduced in 2014 and significantly expanded since February 2022, cover trade, finance, energy, technology, dual-use goods, industry, transport and luxury goods, including the ban on imports of seaborne crude oil and certain petroleum products, the exclusion of Russian banks from SWIFT and the immobilisation of Russian central bank assets of around EUR 210 billion. Renewal requires unanimity: Hungary had threatened for weeks to block the extension and lifted its objection after receiving a declaration on its energy security following the end of gas transit through Ukraine. Since February 2022 the EU has adopted 15 sanctions packages; a 16th package is being prepared for the third anniversary of the invasion on 24 February 2025. Switzerland, which aligns with EU sanctions, had added 54 individuals and 30 entities to its Russia list on 23 December 2024.

evidence.title: OFAC sanctions Chinese firm linked to Salt Typhoon telecom hacks and hacker involved in US Treasury breach
evidence.content: On 17 January 2025 the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned Yin Kecheng, a Shanghai-based cyber actor affiliated with China's Ministry of State Security, for his involvement in the recent compromise of the Treasury Department's Departmental Offices network, which Treasury had detected on 8 December 2024. OFAC also designated Sichuan Juxinhe Network Technology, a cybersecurity company with direct involvement in the Salt Typhoon group, which recently compromised the network infrastructure of multiple major US telecommunication and internet service providers, including AT&T and Verizon, to access private communications. Treasury described the intrusions as an example of an increasing number of PRC state-backed cyber activities that require costly remediation; the action follows the designation of Integrity Technology Group on 3 January for its role in the Flax Typhoon intrusions. All property of the designated persons in the United States is blocked.

evidence.content: The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady at 4.25-4.50% at the January 28-29, 2025 FOMC meeting. evidence.title: BIS Innovation Hub sets out 2025–26 work programme: AI-enabled supervision and green finance
evidence.content: On 14 January 2025 the Bank for International Settlements published the 2025–26 work programme of its Innovation Hub. At the start of 2025 the Hub's portfolio comprised 26 active projects, with 31 projects completed since its establishment in 2019 and 16 new projects started in 2024. The first two new projects of 2025 will develop AI-enabled tools, one to support financial regulation and supervision (suptech) and one for green finance. The Hub's ongoing work on tokenisation and next-generation financial market infrastructure includes the Project Agorá initiative with seven central banks and more than 40 private financial firms exploring tokenised correspondent banking for cross-border payments, and aims to exploit synergies across the existing project portfolio. The Hub serves as a focal point for a network of central bank innovation experts; its Swiss Centre is hosted in Zurich in cooperation with the Swiss National Bank.

evidence.title: FSB Work Programme for 2025
evidence.content: The FSB published its Work Programme for 2025 on 23 January 2025, outlining key regulatory and financial stability priorities for the year. Priority areas: (1) Supporting global cooperation on financial stability; (2) Enhancing resilience of non-bank financial intermediation (NBFI) while preserving its benefits – major G20 deliverable; (3) Harnessing benefits of digital innovation (crypto-assets, AI in finance, cross-border payments) while containing risks – major G20 deliverable; (4) Implementing the systemically important financial institution (SIFI) framework; (5) Addressing financial risks from climate change – climate roadmap progress; (6) Enhancing cross-border payments; (7) Completing resolution reforms. Key G20 deliverables planned: NBFI leverage policy recommendations (Jul 2025); Vulnerabilities from AI in finance (Oct 2025); Thematic peer review on crypto-assets (Oct 2025); FSB Annual Report (Dec 2025). Context: FSB is chaired by Klaas Knot (DNB). Secretariat in Basel, hosted by BIS.

evidence.title: Confirmed: 2024 was the hottest year on record, says UN weather agency
evidence.content: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) confirmed on 10 January 2025 that 2024 was the warmest year on record, based on six international datasets. The global average surface temperature was 1.55 °C (±0.13 °C) above the 1850–1900 average, which means the world has likely experienced the first calendar year more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels. The past ten years, 2015–2024, are the ten warmest on record, and ocean heat content reached a new record. 'Climate history is playing out before our eyes', said WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo, citing devastating extreme weather, rising sea levels and melting ice. WMO stressed that a single year above 1.5 °C does not mean that the long-term Paris Agreement goal, measured over decades, has been missed, but that every fraction of a degree of warming increases impacts on lives, economies and the planet. UN Secretary-General António Guterres called on governments to deliver new national climate action plans in 2025.

evidence.title: Munich Re: natural disasters caused USD 140 billion of insured losses in 2024 as Los Angeles wildfires start 2025
evidence.content: According to the reinsurer Munich Re's annual natural catastrophe report of 9 January 2025, natural disasters caused overall losses of USD 320 billion in 2024 (2023: USD 268 billion), of which USD 140 billion were insured – the third-highest insured total since 1980, the highest since 2017 and almost 50% above the ten-year average. Weather-related events accounted for 93% of overall and 97% of insured losses; hurricanes Helene and Milton in the United States were the costliest events, and 'non-peak' perils such as floods, wildfires and severe thunderstorms caused USD 136 billion of losses, about USD 67 billion of them insured. About 11,000 people died in natural disasters. 'Climate change is showing its claws', Munich Re said. The report was published as wildfires were destroying large parts of Los Angeles, threatening to become the costliest wildfire on record; California prohibited insurers from cancelling or not renewing home policies in the affected areas. With mounting claims, the cost of reinsurance is rising.

evidence.title: Swiss foreign trade 2024: record exports driven almost entirely by chemicals and pharmaceuticals
evidence.content: The Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS/BAZG) reported on 30 January 2025 that Swiss exports rose by 3.2% (real: +2.5%) to a record CHF 282.9 billion in 2024, after declines in both directions of trade in 2023. The record was achieved almost exclusively by the chemical-pharmaceutical sector, whose exports grew by 10.0% (medicines +7.7%) and which accounts for more than half of total exports; exports of chemical-pharmaceutical raw and basic materials doubled within a year. Most other product groups recorded falling foreign sales: watch exports declined by 2.8% and jewellery by 4.5% after record years. Imports fell by 1.6% to CHF 222.3 billion, with imports from Asia at their lowest level since 2020. The opposing trends resulted in a record trade surplus of CHF 60.6 billion. The concentration on a single sector makes Swiss exports sensitive to sector-specific trade policy measures such as tariffs on pharmaceuticals.

evidence.title: UK 30-year gilt yields rise to highest level since 1998 amid concerns over public finances
evidence.content: UK long-term borrowing costs rose to their highest level in more than a quarter of a century in early January 2025. On 7 January the Debt Management Office auctioned GBP 2.25 billion of 30-year gilts at a yield of 5.198%, and the 30-year yield climbed to 5.37% on 8 January, the highest since 1998 and above the levels of the 2022 'mini-budget' crisis; the 10-year yield rose to around 4.8–4.9%, the highest since 2008. Sterling fell to about USD 1.22, its lowest since November 2023. The sell-off was part of a global rise in long-dated government bond yields led by US Treasuries, but was amplified by near-record UK debt issuance of about GBP 297 billion in the 2024–25 fiscal year, persistent inflation and economic stagnation. Analysts warned that higher interest costs could erase the GBP 9.9 billion of fiscal headroom left by the October budget, forcing Chancellor Rachel Reeves to cut spending or raise taxes again; the Treasury said the fiscal rules are 'non-negotiable'.

scenarios_v2.title: Cheaper AI from outside the US could pressure Swiss rates
scenarios_v2.narration:
If advanced AI models from outside the United States spread quickly, they could shake confidence in highly valued US technology shares. Investors in those firms, and pension funds holding them, would face losses. This trigger is hypothetical because the spread of non-US AI remains early and lightly evidenced.

A sharp tech selloff could lead leveraged investors to sell other assets and unwind cross-border positions, spreading pressure across global markets. When investors avoid risk, they might buy Swiss francs as a safe haven, pushing the currency higher. A stronger franc would lower import prices and suppress Swiss inflation. It could limit how much the central bank can cut interest rates to support households and businesses.

Wider disruption would require sustained capital inflows into the franc and a central bank unwilling or unable to offset the rise. The Swiss National Bank has said it remains willing to intervene in foreign exchange markets, which could contain the pressure. Low inflation would also give policymakers room to act.

Before the sell-off Nvidia traded at nearly 60 times earnings, compared with 22 for the S&P 500; the sell-off raised questions about the valuations and the very large AI investment plans of US technology firms.

evidence.content: The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady at 4.25-4.50% at the January 28-29, 2025 FOMC meeting. evidence.title: Swiss foreign trade 2024: record exports driven almost entirely by chemicals and pharmaceuticals
evidence.content: The Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS/BAZG) reported on 30 January 2025 that Swiss exports rose by 3.2% (real: +2.5%) to a record CHF 282.9 billion in 2024, after declines in both directions of trade in 2023. The record was achieved almost exclusively by the chemical-pharmaceutical sector, whose exports grew by 10.0% (medicines +7.7%) and which accounts for more than half of total exports; exports of chemical-pharmaceutical raw and basic materials doubled within a year. Most other product groups recorded falling foreign sales: watch exports declined by 2.8% and jewellery by 4.5% after record years. Imports fell by 1.6% to CHF 222.3 billion, with imports from Asia at their lowest level since 2020. The opposing trends resulted in a record trade surplus of CHF 60.6 billion. The concentration on a single sector makes Swiss exports sensitive to sector-specific trade policy measures such as tariffs on pharmaceuticals.

evidence.title: CBOE VIX volatility index: January 2025 monthly average of 16.76 (range 14.85–19.54)
evidence.content: According to the CBOE VIX daily history, the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX), which measures expected 30-day volatility of the S&P 500, closed at an average of 16.76 in January 2025, within a range of 14.85 to 19.54 over 22 trading days. Implied equity volatility thus stayed close to its long-term median despite the change of US administration and announcements on tariffs; readings above 30 are usually associated with market stress.
